  function initializeReadingPreferences() {

    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }

    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Existing Visual-Language Models (VLMs) have achieved significant progress by being trained on massive-scale datasets, typically under the assumption that data are independent and identically distributed (IID). However, in real-world scenarios, it is often impractical to expect that all data processed by an AI system satisfy this assumption. Furthermore, failure to appropriately handle out-of-distribution (OOD) objects may introduce safety risks in real-world applications (<span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">e.g.</span>, autonomous driving or medical assistance). Unfortunately, current research has not yet provided valid benchmarks that can comprehensively assess the performance of VLMs in response to OOD data. Therefore, we propose <span id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">OODBench</span>, a predominantly automated method with minimal human verification, for constructing new benchmarks and evaluating the ability of VLMs to process OOD data. OODBench contains 40K instance-level OOD instance–category pairs, and we show that current VLMs still exhibit notable performance degradation on OODBench, even when the underlying image categories are common. In addition, we propose a reliable automated assessment metric that employs a Basic-to-Advanced Progression of prompted questions to assess the impact of OOD data on questions of varying difficulty more fully. Lastly, we summarize substantial findings and insights to facilitate future research in the acquisition and evaluation of OOD data <span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
          <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
          
          
          
          
          
          
          
        The dataset is open to the public for research. <a href="https://anonymous.4open.science/r/ood-1B0E" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://anonymous.4open.science/r/ood-1B0E</a></span></span></span>.</p>
  
</div><span id="id1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_affiliationnotice"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">affiliationnotice: </span>Equal contribution</span></span></span>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Recently, Visual-Language Models, VLMs (<span id="S1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">e.g.</span>, GPT-4o <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Achiam et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hurst et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, Gemini <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Team et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, LLaVA family <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>, InternVL family <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024c</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024a</a>)</cite>, Qwen2-VL family <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024a</a>)</cite>, Llama-3.2-Vision <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dubey et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, DeepSeek-VL <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, <span id="S1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">etc.</span>) have demonstrated strong performance across multiple domains. Trained on large-scale multimodal data, these models show strong potential across a range of application scenarios.
These results have led to a common perception that large-scale VLMs exhibit strong generalization capabilities. However, comparatively little attention has been paid to the performance of these VLMs under out-of-distribution (OOD) conditions. The neglect of this issue is partly attributed to the lack of OOD evaluation benchmarks.
Therefore, we construct a benchmark to evaluate the performance of VLMs on OOD data, thereby advancing the progress of VLMs in OOD research and taking a critical step towards realizing intelligent systems that can operate safely in the real world.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18094v1/OODdefine5.png" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/188;" width="476" height="188" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S1.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Comparison of differences in ID data, covariate shift OOD data, and semantic shift data.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In this paper, we consider OOD data as samples that do not belong to the training data distribution.
As shown in Fig. <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, OOD data can be classified into two categories according to the different forms of distributional changes: a data distribution shift where labels-alter, known as <span id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">semantic shift</span>, and a shift where labels remain the same but the data distribution changes, also known as <span id="S1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">covariate shift</span>. The OOD data are essentially associated with the model, as it relies on the models’ assumptions and learned distributions made during the training process. However, most of the mainstream VLMs are closed-source or only open to model parameters, which prevents us from directly accessing the training distributions of these models. Therefore, how to collect OOD data outside of these model training data distributions presents a fundamental challenge.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In the traditional OOD literature <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al. (2024a)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hendrycks et al. (2022)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. (2022)</a></cite>, these studies usually train models on datasets with known categories and obtain OOD test benchmarks by constructing new category data based on the categories in the training data, thus OOD data are different from the original categories, <span id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">i.e.</span>, semantic shift OOD data. However, considering the training category agnostic of existing VLMs, this experimental setting is obviously no longer applicable. Moreover, the ill-pursuit to collecting rarely unseen data ensures neither the rigor of semantic shift OOD data nor real-world significance. For this reason, our work focuses on collecting covariate shift OOD data to construct OOD benchmarks. The approach is based on the assumption that existing VLMs are likely to have been trained on the most common classes of data.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Recent OOD research <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Averly and Chao (2023)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al. (2024b)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jaeger et al. (2023)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Guérin et al. (2023)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhu et al. (2024)</a></cite> has shifted the focus from new category detection to failure detection scenarios, in which the OOD detector is expected to recognize misclassified samples. In this approach, candidate samples that fail to be classified are labeled as OOD data, and samples that are correctly classified are labeled as ID data to enhance the safety and reliability of deep learning models in real-world applications. Building upon this line of work, we further define two categories of OOD data for VLMs from a human perception perspective: <span id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">1) Objects in images that are neither main objects nor semantically related to the main semantic object; 2) Variants or anomalous forms of target objects.</span> The underlying intuition is that VLM training heavily relies on the main semantic objects in images, paying limited attention to non-main semantic objects and their variants/anomalies. This constitutes the OOD in VLM semantic learning. Based on this definition, we first divide the data using an OOD detector, followed by manual spot-checking to ensure the final classification aligns with the proposed OOD definition. Notably, this model-based classification depends on the specific OOD detector employed. VLMs themselves should serve as OOD detectors for classifying OOD data. However, testing each VLM on distinct datasets to identify its specific OOD data is computationally and temporally intensive, making it impractical. Therefore, we propose an automated OOD data classification method supplemented by human verification, which maximizes quality while minimizing manual effort.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">In the design, we adopt a generalized OOD detector instead of a model-specific VLM detector to reduce computational and time costs. Meanwhile, to alleviate the deviation of OOD data division caused by generalized detectors, we introduce a cross-validation scheme with multiple generalized OOD detectors. For implementation, we have chosen off-the-shelf VLMs such as CLIP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Radford et al., 2021</a>)</cite> and BLIP2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2023b</a>)</cite> as generalized OOD detectors and defined the intersection of OOD data detected by both as OOD-Hard data; the data obtained from symmetric difference are defined as OOD-Simple data, denoted as OOD-H and OOD-S, respectively. It is worth noting that CLIP and BLIP2 are essentially replaceable in our OOD division pipeline: any sufficiently robust classifier can serve as a generalized OOD detector and yield comparable results. In the Appendix, we discuss the implications of using different classifiers as generalized OOD detectors in detail. Based on our assumptions, the VLMs have been trained in most of the common data categories. In other words, the OOD data and training data share the same label space, and thus, the divided OOD data can be summarized as covariate shift OOD. We collected the initial benchmark<span id="footnote2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">2</span>
            
            
            
            
            
            
            
          In Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Collection Details ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>, we demonstrate the data distribution of the initial benchmark and the detailed performance of different models tested on this benchmark.</span></span></span> from a publicly available dataset, which contains about 77k yes-or-no samples. To further reduce the testing time, we randomly downsampled the initial benchmark to obtain the main benchmark OODBench.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F2" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18094v1/SubsetPieChart.svg" id="S1.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:124/125;" width="124" height="125"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>: </span><span id="S1.F2.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Distribution of categories and fields in <span id="S1.F2.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">OODBench</span>.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Fig. <a href="#S1.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> illustrates the sample distribution of OODBench, which contains about 40k yes-or-no samples, where OOD-S is 22k and OOD-H is 18k. To evaluate VLM performance on OOD data from multiple dimensions, we propose the ’Basic-Advanced Process Metric’, which evaluates their ability in image understanding, quantity perception, and logical reasoning, respectively.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Our main contributions can be summarized as the following three: 1) We propose a succinct and efficient OOD data division process that is primarily automated and supplemented with lightweight human validation, thereby minimizing labor cost while reducing computational and time overheads. 2) We propose the OOD benchmark for VLMs, which consists of an OOD dataset, an OOD data division pipeline for VLMs, a ‘Basic-to-Advanced Procession Metric‘, and a complete set of experimental procedures. 3) We evaluate eight SOTA VLMs on OODBench, and demonstrate through a large number of experiments that current VLMs still perform poorly when confronted with OOD data, even though the classes of these OOD data are pretty common in natural scenarios.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Out-of-Distribution.</span>
Out-of-distribution (OOD) detection aims to recognize inputs sampled from a distribution different from the model’s training data <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Averly and Chao, 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>. Traditional OOD research mainly focuses on semantic shift (S-OOD), where novel classes arise, yet covariate shift (C-OOD)—where labels remain the same but inputs deviate—can be equally disruptive <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2024a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Salehi et al., 2021</a>)</cite>. In safety-critical fields like autonomous driving, even minor shifts may cause severe misclassifications and catastrophic results.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">While robust models may correctly handle such shifts, weaker models often benefit from rejecting uncertain samples to mitigate high-risk errors <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2021</a>)</cite>. Reflecting this, OOD research has gradually shifted from purely detecting unseen classes to failure detection, encompassing both semantic and covariate shifts that can cause misclassification <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wiles et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2021</a>)</cite>. Nevertheless, there remains limited exploration of how modern Vision-Language Models (VLMs) contend with these conditions. Our work addresses this gap by constructing an OOD benchmark for VLMs, emphasizing common categories that remain challenging under real-world variation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Multimodal Large Language Models &amp; Benchmark.</span>
Recent Vision-Language Models (VLMs) trained on massive image-text corpora have achieved impressive gains in tasks like visual reasoning, captioning, and Q&amp;A <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2023b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Team et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Achiam et al., 2023</a>)</cite>. Notable examples include GPT-4 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Achiam et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hurst et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, Gemini <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Team et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, LLaVA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>, and InternVL <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024c</a>)</cite>, often leveraging large-scale datasets such as LAION <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schuhmann et al., 2022</a>)</cite> and MS COCO <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al., 2014</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Although benchmarks like MMBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, SeedBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2023a</a>)</cite>, and GQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hudson and Manning, 2019</a>)</cite> assess general vision-language performance, they mainly cover in-distribution cases and rarely address out-of-distribution (OOD) data. For example, SeedBench offers 19K multiple-choice questions across images and videos, highlighting model limits but rarely exploring out-of-distribution scenarios. To fill the gap, we introduce OODBench, testing VLM robustness under covariate shift. By incorporating simple and hard OOD categories and employing a “Basic-to-Advanced” protocol, OODBench reveals key weaknesses in current models and encourages future work on safer, more reliable multimodal systems.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">While OOD data can trigger hallucinations, not all hallucinations arise from distribution shifts. Benchmarks like HallusionBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Guan et al., 2024</a>)</cite> study language and visual hallucinations, whereas OODBench systematically applies covariate shifts to measure genuine OOD resilience.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Existing Definitions and Formulations</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Out-of-distribution (OOD) refers to samples that originate from a data distribution distinct from that of the training set. Given a VLM <math id="S3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>f</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> trained on data sampled from the distribution <math id="S3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{\text{tr}}(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Y}\in\mathcal{S})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mtext>tr</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒴</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{\text{tr}}(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Y}\in\mathcal{S})</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{X}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{X}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes training samples, <math id="S3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{Y}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒴</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{Y}</annotation></semantics></math> the corresponding labels, and <math id="S3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{S}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{S}</annotation></semantics></math> the label space. This training distribution is referred to as the in-distribution (ID). In contrast, common OOD data can be divided into two types: covariate shifts (<span id="S3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">i.e.</span>, labels remain unchanged, involving only samples from the training class) and semantic shifts (<span id="S3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">i.e.</span>, labels change, involving only samples from the novel category).

<br class="ltx_break"><span id="S3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Semantic Shift.</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib73" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lipton et al. (2018)</a></cite> In a traditional experimental setup, the semantic shift data consists of novel category samples outside of the model labeling space <math id="S3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{S}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{S}</annotation></semantics></math>. The semantic shift data consists of a novel category of samples. Given semantic labels <math id="S3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Y_{\text{tr}}\in\mathcal{Y}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>Y</mi><mtext>tr</mtext></msub><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒴</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Y_{\text{tr}}\in\mathcal{Y}</annotation></semantics></math> from the training distribution and semantic labels <math id="S3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Y_{\text{te}}\in\mathcal{Y}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>Y</mi><mtext>te</mtext></msub><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒴</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Y_{\text{te}}\in\mathcal{Y}</annotation></semantics></math> from the testing distribution, where <math id="S3.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Y_{\text{tr}}\cap Y_{\text{te}}=\emptyset" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>Y</mi><mtext>tr</mtext></msub><mo>∩</mo><msub><mi>Y</mi><mtext>te</mtext></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∅</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Y_{\text{tr}}\cap Y_{\text{te}}=\emptyset</annotation></semantics></math> and satisfy <math id="S3.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{\text{tr}}(y)=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mtext>tr</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{\text{tr}}(y)=0</annotation></semantics></math> for all <math id="S3.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y\in Y_{\text{te}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi>Y</mi><mtext>te</mtext></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y\in Y_{\text{te}}</annotation></semantics></math>.
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="S3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Covariate Shift.</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib74" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shimodaira (2000)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib73" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lipton et al. (2018)</a></cite> The covariate shift data consists of samples from the model label space <math id="S3.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{S}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{S}</annotation></semantics></math> but from different domains. In other words, the image distributions of the training and test data are different: <math id="S3.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{\text{tr}}(x)\neq P_{\text{te}}(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mtext>tr</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≠</mo><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mtext>te</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{\text{tr}}(x)\neq P_{\text{te}}(x)</annotation></semantics></math>, but the label distributions remain the same: <math id="S3.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{\text{tr}}(y|x)=P_{\text{te}}(y|x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mtext>tr</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mtext>te</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{\text{tr}}(y|x)=P_{\text{te}}(y|x)</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>The OODBench</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">VLMs have demonstrated outstanding performance across multiple tasks and domains, profoundly reshaping the landscape of AI development. However, their performance when encountering OOD data remains under-evaluated. Existing VLMs typically use agnostic training categories and collect rare categories as semantic shift OOD data, which do not accurately assess model performance on OOD categories encountered in real-world applications, as these rare categories may not represent common OOD types. To remedy this shortcoming, we focus on collecting covariate shift OOD data for constructing OODBench. Specifically, the OOD data categories need to be broadly representative to ensure their real-world relevance. Meanwhile, OOD data in certain scenarios can severely degrade model performance, potentially causing catastrophic outcomes (<span id="S4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">e.g.</span>, autonomous driving). Thus, we collected data for two key scenarios: natural scenarios (COCO <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al., 2014</a>)</cite>, LVIS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gupta et al., 2019</a>)</cite>) and autonomous driving (nuScenes <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Caesar et al., 2020</a>)</cite>, Cityscapes <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cordts et al., 2016</a>)</cite>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Our goal is to build an instance-level OOD benchmark for VLMs. To this end, we define OOD data from the perspective of VLMs’ semantic learning: 1) Objects in images that are neither main objects nor semantically related to the main semantic object; 2) Variants or anomalous forms of target objects. However, manually screening each instance object that meets the above definition is practically infeasible. To address this issue, we designed a concise and effective OOD data division process, whose overall framework is illustrated in Fig. <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 4 The OODBench ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>. Specifically, We strictly follow the definition of OOD data division as defined in previous approaches  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Averly and Chao, 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2024b</a>)</cite> and label the model-specified misclassified examples as OOD data to improve the safety and reliability of the deep learning model in real-world applications. The underlying intuition is that, taking CLIP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Radford et al., 2021</a>)</cite> as an example, its large-scale contrastive learning mechanism naturally forms a clustering structure in the image-text embedding space during training, grouping ”main semantic objects” and ”typical forms.” In contrast, non-main semantic objects, semantic variants, or anomalous forms typically exhibit significant deviations within this space. Therefore, when an image is paired with text describing non-primary semantic content, the unstable or erroneous predictions generated by CLIP fundamentally reflect that “the current semantic distribution of the image-text pair has deviated from its training distribution.” We leverage this anomaly in semantic distance manifested within the embedding space as an auxiliary signal to identify potential OOD candidate samples. Given an image <math id="S4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> and all candidate category labels <math id="S4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y=\{y_{1},\dots,y_{i},\dots,y_{n}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y=\{y_{1},\dots,y_{i},\dots,y_{n}\}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S4.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the <math id="S4.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>-th label and <math id="S4.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> is the total number of category labels (<span id="S4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">e.g.</span>, the number of category labels in the COCO dataset <math id="S4.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n=80" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>80</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n=80</annotation></semantics></math>). We input both images and labels into the off-the-shelf pretrained OOD detector to obtain logits of <math id="S4.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(x,y)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(x,y)</annotation></semantics></math> pairs.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Purify.</span> Since an image may correspond to multiple labels, we note that the corresponding label of the image is <math id="S4.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y_{i}^{x}\in y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>x</mi></msubsup><mo>∈</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y_{i}^{x}\in y</annotation></semantics></math>. Direct softmax operation on logits may lead to interference between labels because softmax assumes that each sample can only belong to one category, which makes the final image-category matching probability not accurately reflect the actual probability. For example, when an image contains both <span id="S4.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">cat</span> and <span id="S4.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">dog</span> categories, softmax calculates the probability by comparing the scores of each category with the scores of the other categories. Therefore, the logits of cat and dog will interact with each other after softmax, which may lead to inaccurate classification results as the cat’s score decreases due to the dog’s score and vice versa. To address this issue, we introduce the purify operation to eliminate the interaction between different <math id="S4.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y^{x}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>y</mi><mi>x</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y^{x}</annotation></semantics></math>. In the implementation, we select one of the <math id="S4.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y^{x}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>y</mi><mi>x</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y^{x}</annotation></semantics></math> as the current category and set the logits of the other <math id="S4.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y^{x}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>y</mi><mi>x</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y^{x}</annotation></semantics></math> to negative infinity, thus eliminating the interference of other labels on the selected label.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p4.1" class="ltx_p">After the <span id="S4.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">purify</span> operation, we obtained the <math id="S4.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(x,y)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(x,y)</annotation></semantics></math> match probability of the selected labels that are not interfered with by other labeling categories. Subsequently, we perform OOD data collection based on this match probability. In our setting, failure detection is divided into two cases. The first case is that the probability of the category <math id="S4.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y^{\prime}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>y</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y^{\prime}</annotation></semantics></math> that does not exist on the image is higher than the probability of all label categories <math id="S4.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y^{x}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>y</mi><mi>x</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y^{x}</annotation></semantics></math>, <span id="S4.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">i.e</span>., <math id="S4.p4.m4" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="P(x,y^{\prime}|y^{\prime}\in y,y^{\prime}\notin y^{x})&gt;P(x,y^{x})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>y</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><msup><mi>y</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>∈</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>y</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>∉</mo><msup><mi>y</mi><mi>x</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>y</mi><mi>x</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(x,y^{\prime}|y^{\prime}\in y,y^{\prime}\notin y^{x})&gt;P(x,y^{x})</annotation></semantics></math>. The second case is that the probability of the labeling category <math id="S4.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y^{x}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>y</mi><mi>x</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y^{x}</annotation></semantics></math> of the current image <math id="S4.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> is lower than a hyperparameter threshold <math id="S4.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math>, <span id="S4.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">i.e.</span>, <math id="S4.p4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P(x,y^{x})&lt;T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>y</mi><mi>x</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(x,y^{x})&lt;T</annotation></semantics></math>. By filtering the samples that satisfy these two cases, we have successfully acquired the instance-level OOD data. However, the OOD data collected by the model-specified approach is closely related to the OOD detectors. To mitigate the OOD division bias introduced by these detectors and their potential classification errors, while collecting OOD data with greater real-world adaptability and universality, thereby enhancing model reliability in practical applications, we introduce a cross-validation approach with multiple generalized OOD detectors. In implementation, we chose CLIP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Radford et al., 2021</a>)</cite> and BLIP2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2023b</a>)</cite> as OOD detectors and defined the intersection of OOD data divided by the two models as OOD-Hard data, while the symmetric difference of data divided by the two models is defined as OOD-Simple data. After completing the OOD data division, we further conducted manual sampling inspections to ensure that the division strictly conformed to our definition of OOD. The experimental results show that the OOD data classified by our proposed OODBench can effectively approximate the actual OOD distribution faced by large VLMs. Users can easily collect and extend OOD data through this process for applications in different fields. Our experiments demonstrate that, despite the prevalence of these OOD data classes in real-world scenarios, current state-of-the-art VLMs still struggle with out-of-distribution inputs. Even the GPT-4o achieves only approximately <math id="S4.p4.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="65\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>65</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">65\%</annotation></semantics></math> accuracy on OOD-H data, compared to over <math id="S4.p4.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="90\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>90</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">90\%</annotation></semantics></math> on in-distribution samples.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F3" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18094v1/Pipeline1.png" id="S4.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:381/158;" width="381" height="158" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F3.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 3</span>: </span><span id="S4.F3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Pipeline of OOD data collection.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S4.F4" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18094v1/conservation.png" id="S4.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:381/74;" width="381" height="74" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F4.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 4</span>: </span><span id="S4.F4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Basic-to-Advanced Progression Metric Example. Basic-to-Advanced Progression Metric covers three problems: existential, counting, and logical reasoning problems from top to bottom.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Basic-to-Advanced Progression (BAP) Metric.</span>
Through the above process, we divide the OOD data at the instance level. To comprehensively evaluate the impact of OOD data on VLMs from different dimensions, we meticulously devised the Basic-to-Advanced Progression Metric. Specifically, as shown in Fig. <a href="#S4.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 4 The OODBench ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, we examine the recognition ability, counting perception ability, and reasoning ability of VLMs by constructing existential, counting, and logical reasoning problems. The existential question is the essential reasoning task. It is usually the precursor to other questions, which require the model to make a judgment about whether a particular category of objects is present in the image. The counting problem is a further judgment about the number of objects in the image after the model has correctly answered the existential question. This stage requires the model to return a specific numerical value rather than a simple ‘yes‘ or ‘no‘. In the third stage, we evaluate the reasoning ability of the model by asking questions about different objects in the same image (<span id="S4.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">e.g.</span>, <span id="S4.p5.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Is the number of [class 1] in the image greater than the number of [class 2]? Answer with ‘yes‘ or ‘no‘</span>). Logical reasoning problems build on counting problems, which require the model to be aware not only of the number of objects in each category but also of making comparisons between the number of categories. Progressive questioning helps to improve the interpretability of the model’s reasoning process. Each step of the answer is based on clear logic, which helps the user understand the thinking process of the model. Finally, we calculated <math id="S4.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C/N\times 100\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mrow><mn>100</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C/N\times 100\%</annotation></semantics></math> as the BAP Metric, where <math id="S4.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math> is the number of questions answered correctly, and <math id="S4.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> is the total number of questions.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Experiment</h2>

<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1 </span>Selected Datasets</h3>

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">COCO. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al., 2014</a>)</cite>.</span> The COCO dataset is a widely used natural image dataset in computer vision. It contains over 330,000 images across 80 categories (<span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">e.g.</span>, people, animals, vehicles, <span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">etc.</span>). We chose its 2017 version validation set as the source of OODBench metadata.
<span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">LVIS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gupta et al., 2019</a>)</cite>.</span> The LVIS dataset is a large-scale natural scene dataset that focuses on instance segmentation. Especially, it focuses on the recognition of fine-grained categories and provides rich instance-level annotations.
<span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">nuScenes <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Caesar et al., 2020</a>)</cite>.</span> nuScenes is a large-scale autonomous driving dataset that provides 360-degree views of city streets, covering a wide range of urban environments and road conditions. The dataset provides camera, LiDAR, and radar sensor data. To control the benchmark’s sample number, we selected 6,019 keyframes from the front camera in the validation set as metadata for nuScenes.
<span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Cityscapes <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cordts et al., 2016</a>)</cite>.</span> Cityscapes is an autonomous driving dataset focused on urban street scenes for scene understanding. We chose images from the camera on the left side of the validation set as metadata for Cityscapes. In addition, we adjusted labels to ensure that their expressions conform to natural language conventions and excluded potentially ambiguous labels. For more details, please refer to Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Collection Details ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F5" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18094v1/question.png" id="S5.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:381/151;" width="381" height="151" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S5.F5.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 5</span>: </span><span id="S5.F5.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">The <span id="S5.F5.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">OODBench</span> example has two questions and one instance, with the answers alternated to avoid the model being over-scored due to biased output distribution.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.2 </span>Evaluation Setup</h3>

<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In our main results, in order to comprehensively evaluate the performance of the model, we selected several commonly used evaluation metrics, including Accuracy, F1 Score, Precision, Recall, and Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC). In addition, in the experiments of BAP Metric, we introduced three additional metrics to refine the evaluation further. Specifically, we define the ‘Existential Accuracy‘ (E-Acc) metric, where a point is awarded only if the model correctly answers the existential question. The ‘Counting Accuracy‘ (C-Acc) metric, on the other hand, requires the model to obtain a point only when it correctly answers the number of specified categories in the image. Finally, we award a point for ‘Logical Accuracy‘ (L-Acc) when the model correctly answers both counting and logical questions in the test sample. Regarding the OOD detectors and the hyperparameter <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math>, we conducted systematic ablation studies to determine the optimal value of <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> as well as the type and number of generalized OOD detectors. Detailed analyses of their impact on performance are provided in Appendix <a href="#A5" title="Appendix E Ablation Study of the Generalized OOD Detector and Hyperparameter T ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E</span></a>.</p>
</div>

All models perform significantly lower on OOD-H than on ID. The performance of the latest models, such as LLaVA-NeXT, Llama3.2-Vision, InternVL2.5, and Qwen2-VL, lags behind the ID data by about <math id="S5.T1.m40" class="ltx_Math" alttext="20\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>20</mn><mo mathsize="1.110em">%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">20\%</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S5.T1.m41" class="ltx_Math" alttext="30\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>30</mn><mo mathsize="1.110em">%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">30\%</annotation></semantics></math> on OOD-H data. Even the best closed-source model, GPT-4o, still performs <math id="S5.T1.m42" class="ltx_Math" alttext="26\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>26</mn><mo mathsize="1.110em">%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">26\%</annotation></semantics></math> lower on OOD-H than ID.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.3 </span>Main Results Analysis</h3>

<div id="S5.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Through our OOD data collection process, we divide instance-level OOD data into distinct subsets. We define the intersection of OOD data identified by multiple OOD detectors as OOD-H, and the symmetric difference as OOD-S. Based on this process, ID data are obtained by randomly pairing images and categories and excluding pairs identified as OOD. As shown in Fig. <a href="#S5.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 5.1 Selected Datasets ‣ 5 Experiment ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, we present two questions for each instance respectively (<span id="S5.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Does this image <span id="S5.SS3.p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">contain</span> a [class]? (yes or no)</span> and <span id="S5.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Does this image <span id="S5.SS3.p1.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">not contain</span> a [class]? (yes or no)</span>) and assign the opposite label to each question. This strategy effectively balances the label distributions of different instance data. It mitigates the tendency of VLMs to favor either ‘yes‘ or ‘no‘ responses due to training data bias. As the task format superficially resembles prompt templates used in some hallucination detection work, we systematically compare hallucination data with OODBench in Appendix <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D Differences between OODBench and Hallucination ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a> across three dimensions—definition, generation mechanism, and experimental results—to clarify their fundamental differences.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Tab. <a href="#S5.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 5.2 Evaluation Setup ‣ 5 Experiment ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> shows the performance of the current state-of-the-art LLaVA-NeXT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>, DeepSeek-VL <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, InternVL2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024c</a>)</cite>, InternVL2.5 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024a</a>)</cite>, Llama-3.2-Vision <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dubey et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, Qwen2-VL <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024a</a>)</cite>, Gemini <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Team et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and GPT-4o <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Achiam et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hurst et al., 2024</a>)</cite> models on <span id="S5.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">OODBench</span>. The results indicate that most VLMs exhibit a <math id="S5.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="20\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>20</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">20\%</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S5.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="30\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>30</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">30\%</annotation></semantics></math> accuracy drop on OOD-H data relative to ID data. In addition, all models show a decreasing trend in accuracy on ID, OOD-S, and OOD-H data. Essentially, OOD-S data is data that is only identified as OOD data by one OOD detector and not identified as OOD data by another OOD detector. In contrast, OOD-H data is identified as OOD data by both OOD detectors.
These results show decreasing accuracy on ID, OOD-S, and OOD-H data, suggesting that multiple well-pretrained VLMs are more effective OOD detectors for collecting data aligned with real-world scenarios than a single detector. Moreover, this process requires no extra human effort, minimizing labor costs.
Notably, VLMs (e.g., LLaVA-NeXT, DeepSeek-VL, InternVL2/2.5, Qwen2-VL) show poor recall on OOD-H data, with LLaVA-NeXT and DeepSeek-VL even falling below <math id="S5.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="50\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>50</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">50\%</annotation></semantics></math> random chance. By contrast, recall on ID data remains around <math id="S5.SS3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="90\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>90</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">90\%</annotation></semantics></math>, yielding a <math id="S5.SS3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="26" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>26</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">26</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="S5.SS3.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="43\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>43</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">43\%</annotation></semantics></math> drop on OOD-H.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">These results suggest that instances in OOD data are more likely to be missed than those in ID data. In safety-critical settings, low recall can be particularly problematic. For example, an autonomous driving system must detect all hazards—pedestrians, vehicles, or traffic signs, since missing any can greatly increase accident risk. Appendix <a href="#A6" title="Appendix F OODBench Sub-Dataset Performance ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a> details VLM performance on natural and driving datasets, illustrating how OOD data affect model behavior across scenarios.</p>
</div>

<section id="S5.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.4 </span>Does Chain-of-Thought Reasoning Work on OOD Data?</h3>

<div id="S5.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting encourages models to generate intermediate steps before producing an answer, and has been reported to improve performance on reasoning-style tasks. However, when confronted with OOD data, models often fail to reason accurately using their existing knowledge, as such data fall outside the training distribution. A natural question is whether CoT prompting still helps in these cases. Specifically, does explicitly expanding the inference process help models handle unfamiliar inputs? To investigate this, we add a CoT prompt requiring step-by-step analysis and evaluate whether it improves VLM performance on OOD data. OOur prompt setup mirrors the main experiment, with an added requirement for stepwise analysis: <span id="S5.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">e.g.</span>, <span id="S5.SS4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Does this image contain [class]? Yes or No? Let’s break down the information step by step.</span> and <span id="S5.SS4.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Does this image not contain [class]? Yes or No? Let’s break down the information step by step.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S5.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 5.2 Evaluation Setup ‣ 5 Experiment ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> reports the performance of different VLMs with CoT prompting. Gemini <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Team et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, InternVL2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024c</a>)</cite>, and InternVL2.5 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024a</a>)</cite> exhibit similar improvements: on challenging OOD-H samples, accuracy increases by about 10% over baseline; ID accuracy remains stable or rises slightly; OOD-S accuracy declines by 2–3% on average. Precision gains 15.23%, 22.59%, and 12.46% for Gemini, InternVL2, and InternVL2.5, respectively, while recall is unchanged or marginally lower. In contrast, LLaVA-NeXT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>, Qwen2-VL <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024a</a>)</cite>, and Qwen2.5-VL <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bai et al., 2025a</a>)</cite> show negligible OOD-H gains: Qwen2-VL remains stable on ID and OOD-S, whereas LLaVA-NeXT’s ID accuracy drops from 84.79% to 64.96%. Moreover, GPT-4o <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Achiam et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hurst et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, DeepSeek-VL <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, DeepSeek-VL2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2024a</a>)</cite>, and Llama-3.2-Vision <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dubey et al., 2024</a>)</cite> suffer overall performance degradation after CoT prompting: GPT-4o and Llama-3.2-Vision ID accuracy falls by 13.82% and 18.27%, respectively, and OOD-H accuracy declines by 1.5–5%. Hence, CoT yields negative gains for these models.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F6" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18094v1/error_analysis.png" id="S5.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:381/152;" width="381" height="152" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S5.F6.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 6</span>: </span><span id="S5.F6.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Typical failure cases of GPT-4o on OODBench. Errors primarily fall into two categories: non-main semantic objects and semantic variants.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.5 </span>BAP Evaluation of ID and OOD Data Differences</h3>

<div id="S5.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To assess VLM performance on OOD data across multiple dimensions, we introduce the Basic-to-Advanced Progression (BAP) metric, which evaluates model performance in recognition, counting, and reasoning tasks. Specifically, we define three metrics—Existential Accuracy (E-Acc), Counting Accuracy (C-Acc), and Logical Accuracy (L-Acc)—using a progressive questioning framework to assess existential, counting, and logical challenges, respectively.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For BAP evaluation, we select images containing at least two distinct labels from the ID, OOD-S, and OOD-H datasets. Each image is paired with two distinct category labels (without duplication), forming test samples with paired labels from different categories. The quantity labels for counting tasks are obtained by counting the number of target object instances in the source annotations.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS5.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS5.p3.1" class="ltx_p">As task difficulty increases from E-Acc to C-Acc to L-Acc, all models exhibit a consistent decline in performance. This trend becomes more pronounced as the data distribution shifts from ID to OOD-S and OOD-H, corresponding to increasing divergence from the training distribution and resulting in varying degrees of performance degradation across metrics. Most models achieve robust results on ID data, particularly on E-Acc and C-Acc. However, performance declines as the data transitions to OOD-S and further to OOD-H, with the largest drop observed on L-Acc. On more challenging OOD data (e.g., OOD-H), models exhibit a substantial decrease in logical accuracy.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS5.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS5.p4.1" class="ltx_p">E-Acc mainly tests recognition without complex reasoning. On OOD-H data, GPT-4o <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Achiam et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hurst et al., 2024</a>)</cite> shows the best recognition, correctly identifying category existence in images. In contrast, C-Acc evaluates the ability to count object instances, requiring both recognition and accurate counting. Gemini <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Team et al., 2024</a>)</cite> leads with <math id="S5.SS5.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="42.82\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>42.82</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">42.82\%</annotation></semantics></math>, underscoring its relative strength in counting.
L-Acc evaluates logical reasoning by comparing category counts (e.g., <em id="S5.SS5.p4.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Is A greater than B?</em>). This task couples counting with higher-level reasoning, and all models show a sharp drop in performance, highlighting the challenge of logical reasoning and quantitative relations in OOD settings.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Analysis of Error Cases</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in Figure <a href="#S5.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ 5.4 Does Chain-of-Thought Reasoning Work on OOD Data? ‣ 5 Experiment ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>, we present a qualitative analysis of failure patterns for the representative GPT-4o model on OODBench. Errors primarily cluster into two semantic OOD categories: non-main objects and semantic variants.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(1) Failures caused by non-primary semantic objects.</span> When a clear main semantic object exists in an image (<span id="S6.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">e.g.</span>, ”people” in the first and fourth examples of the first row in Figure <a href="#S5.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ 5.4 Does Chain-of-Thought Reasoning Work on OOD Data? ‣ 5 Experiment ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>), the model’s image–caption pretraining objective tends to emphasize alignment with the main semantic object, while learning about non-main semantic objects is insufficient or even absent. Therefore, when we construct scenarios in OODBench where the main semantic object is present, but the question involves a non-main semantic object, the model appears to lack stable image–text associations for these semantics, leading to consistent mispredictions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(2) Failures due to semantic variants.</span> Another common error category stems from semantic variants. For example, the ”skateboard made of cake” in the first sample of the second row in Figure <a href="#S5.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ 5.4 Does Chain-of-Thought Reasoning Work on OOD Data? ‣ 5 Experiment ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>. During training, the model predominantly encounters “skateboards” with standard appearances drawn from natural image distributions. The joint distribution of images and text forms the model’s default semantic template for the concept of ”skateboard.” When we replace the target object with variants featuring different materials, shapes, or construction methods (such as a ”cake-shaped skateboard”), this sample deviates from the training distribution within the model’s image-text semantic space. Consequently, the model misclassifies or ignores it.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p4.1" class="ltx_p">These qualitative observations suggest that failures under semantic shifts are not random but linked to mismatches between joint image–text distributions and pretrained representations, consistent with our quantitative results.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S7" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">7 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this paper, we introduce <span id="S7.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">OODBench</span> to evaluate the performance of Vision Language Models (VLMs) in the face of out-of-distribution data. OODBench is able to more accurately reflect the coping ability of VLMs when they encounter data distribution shifts in real-world scenarios. In addition, we present the Basic-to-Advanced Progression Metric for evaluating the recognition, count-awareness, and reasoning abilities of VLMs. Our automated OOD division benchmarking process adapts efficiently to new data sources and does not require significant human effort, enabling future evaluations of the ability of vision language models to be out-of-distribution of different domains.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S8" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">8 </span>Impact Statements</h2>

<div id="S8.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This paper presents work whose goal is to advance the field of machine learning. There are many potential societal consequences of our work, none of which we feel must be specifically highlighted here.</p>
</div>
</section>

<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Collection Details</h2>

<div id="A1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Initial Benchmark.</span> Fig. <a href="#A1.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ Appendix A Collection Details ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> illustrates that we collected the initial benchmark from a publicly available dataset, which contains about 77k yes-or-no samples, where OOD-S is 51k and OOD-H is 26k. Due to the large sample size of the benchmarks, to save testing time, we randomly downsampled the OOD-Simple and OOD-Hard category data in the benchmarks with a sample size of more than 6,000 to the <span id="A1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">OODBench</span> to ensure that the sample size of each category did not exceed 6,000.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A1.F7" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18094v1/total_pie.svg" id="A1.F7.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:143/144;" width="143" height="144"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A1.F7.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 7</span>: </span><span id="A1.F7.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Distribution of categories and fields in initial benchmark.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">VLMs for Classification.</span> In terms of implementation details, we input image-question pairs corresponding to OOD samples into multimodal large models to generate textual responses. Subsequently, we convert the model output into binary labels by identifying the keywords ‘yes‘ or ‘no‘ in the generated text. This method has also been applied in the literature <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. In Tab. <a href="#S5.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 5.2 Evaluation Setup ‣ 5 Experiment ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, an average accuracy of 90% is achieved on ID data, which further validates the effectiveness of the method in classification tasks. In the BAP task, we also used this method to obtain the model’s counting prediction results and compare them with the real labels to determine whether the model’s answers to counting questions were accurate.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">nuScenes and Cityscapes dataset label modifications.</span> Since the labels of nuScenes do not conform to natural languages, such as ‘human.pedestrian.adult‘, using the original labels as text directly will cause the OOD detector to fail to understand their meaning, which will fail OOD data division. Therefore, as shown in Table <a href="#A1.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ Appendix A Collection Details ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, we manually convert these labels into a form that conforms to natural language conventions. Meanwhile, since the original label ‘movable object.debris‘ of nuScenes is not clear, we exclude it to avoid ambiguity. Similarly, we also eliminated the background, ambiguous, and semantic duplicates from the Cityscapes labels, and Table <a href="#A1.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ Appendix A Collection Details ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> shows the final labels we retained.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A1.T3" class="ltx_table">
<div id="A1.T3.3" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_center ltx_transformed_outer" style="width:412.6pt;height:176.8pt;vertical-align:-86.9pt;"><span class="ltx_transformed_inner" style="transform:translate(-131.2pt,56.2pt) scale(0.611185099102793,0.611185099102793) ;">
<table id="A1.T3.3.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
<thead class="ltx_thead">
<tr id="A1.T3.3.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="A1.T3.3.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt"><span id="A1.T3.3.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Original Labels</span></th>
<th id="A1.T3.3.1.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt"><span id="A1.T3.3.1.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Modified Labels</span></th>
<th id="A1.T3.3.1.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt"><span id="A1.T3.3.1.1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Remark</span></th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">

<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Statistical Evidence for the OOD Nature of OODBench in Modern MLLMs</h2>

<div id="A2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To verify whether OODBench constitutes OOD data within existing MLLMs, we conducted systematic statistical analysis across two complementary dimensions: open-source models and closed-source models. In the open-source model section, we calculated the semantic overlap rate between the model training corpus and the COCO-train-OOD partition, which was constructed according to the same rules as OODBench. We then evaluated the consistency and robustness of this partition using methods such as exact binomial intervals, Bayesian priors, and Two One-Sided Tests (TOST). In the closed-source model section, we further establish independent chains of evidence based on both the “significance” and “magnitude consistency” of performance results. This is achieved through significance testing for performance degradation (ID <math id="A2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math> OOD) and equivalence assessments against open-source OOD behavioral signatures. Through these complementary statistical inferences from both open-source and closed-source models, we jointly demonstrate that OODBench indeed exhibits verifiable OOD characteristics for current MLLMs, examining both the nature of data distributions and model response behaviors.</p>
</div>
<section id="A2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.1 </span>OOD Evidence from Open-Source Models</h3>

<div id="A2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Open-Source MLLMs refer to models that disclose their core components to varying degrees within the research community, thereby enabling independent auditability, inspectability, reproducibility, or reusability. It is crucial to emphasize that open-source is not a binary attribute but exists along a continuum of openness. As shown in Table <a href="#A2.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ B.1 OOD Evidence from Open-Source Models ‣ Appendix B Statistical Evidence for the OOD Nature of OODBench in Modern MLLMs ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, we categorize current open-source MLLMs into four primary levels based on the scope and granularity of disclosed information, where each level exhibits a hierarchical increase in model weights, architectural details, training code, training data transparency, and reproducibility.</p>
</div>
