<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="A2.T5.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 5</span>: </span><span id="A2.T5.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Current open-source MLLM models are categorized into four primary tiers based on the scope and granularity of publicly disclosed information. Each level exhibits progressively enhanced transparency and reproducibility across model weights, architectural details, training code, training data, and overall reproducibility.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To rigorously assess whether the proposed OODBench constitutes out-of-distribution (OOD) data for existing open-source MLLMs, we conducted a systematic statistical analysis. We first quantified the overlap ratio between OODBench and each model’s corresponding training corpus. Then we incorporated statistical inference procedures to estimate the population-level proportion of OOD samples across models. To enhance the representativeness and cross-model comparability of these evaluations, we adopted the COCO dataset—one of the most commonly used and widely standardized datasets in multimodal model training—as the unified reference source. This provides a consistent framework for estimating overlap ratios and determining the OOD characteristics of our constructed benchmark.</p>
</div>
<section id="A2.SS1.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">B.1.1 </span>Principles for Selecting Model Samples</h4>

<div id="A2.SS1.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We first conducted a systematic survey of current mainstream open-source MLLMs, covering diverse model families, parameter scales, and architectural paradigms. By comprehensively collecting publicly released versions, model repositories, and official documentation, we identified 28 model families corresponding to a candidate set of 93 models spanning parameter sizes from 0.5B to 424B. To ensure transparency and auditability at the training data level, we restricted our selection to robust open-source models at Levels 3 and 4, meaning those that either publicly disclose their training data inventories or possess strict reproducibility. In this process, we excluded the following two categories of models that did not meet these criteria:</p>
<ul id="A2.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="A2.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A2.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Models using in-house or non-public data.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A2.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A2.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Models with incomplete training data lists often lack precise entries, which prevents line-by-line verification.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="A2.T6.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 6</span>: </span><span id="A2.T6.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Complete summary of collected models. Includes models ultimately included in the analysis as well as those excluded during the screening process.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A2.SS1.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">After obtaining a set of candidate models that meet the training data transparency requirements, we further exclude models that did not use COCO as a training data source. Since our objective is to quantify the overlap ratio between OODBench-COCO and each MLLM’s training data, a model with no COCO inclusion in its training corpus would yield a trivially zero overlap ratio. This would render it incapable of providing any meaningful validation for our proposed overlap ratio analysis workflow. Consequently, such models are unsuitable as statistical test samples. After these two rounds of screening, we ultimately obtained 50 qualifying MLLMs for subsequent overlap ratio calculations and statistical inference analysis. Table <a href="#A2.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ B.1.1 Principles for Selecting Model Samples ‣ B.1 OOD Evidence from Open-Source Models ‣ Appendix B Statistical Evidence for the OOD Nature of OODBench in Modern MLLMs ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> provides a comprehensive summary of the collected models, including both those ultimately included in the analysis and those excluded during the screening process.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS1.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">B.1.2 </span>Semantic-Level OOD Pairing and Overlap Rate Analysis</h4>

<div id="A2.SS1.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We first select an image and perform semantic consistency matching for its image-category within the OOD division. Specifically, we collect all annotated versions of this image across various MLLM training corpora (<span id="A2.SS1.SSS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">e.g.</span>, captions, OCR, conversations, detailed descriptions, complex reasoning, REC, REG, grounding, <span id="A2.SS1.SSS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">etc.</span>). We then systematically examine each annotation to determine whether it contains semantic expressions matching the OOD category we assigned. If the category appears in any annotated version, it indicates the model has learned the corresponding image–category semantic relationship, and this image–category pair is considered ID data. Conversely, if the category is absent from all annotated versions, the image–category pair is classified as OOD data at the semantic level of learning. It is important to note that OODBench utilizes the COCO val dataset, while most MLLM training data is based on the COCO train version. These datasets have no overlap at the image level, making it impossible to calculate overlap rates using image matching rules directly. This version discrepancy may result in false-zero overlap. To address this issue, we regenerate OOD data using the COCO train image set, applying the same division criteria as OODBench. We then calculate the overlap rate with each MLLM’s training data based on this division. This approach verifies whether our categorized samples genuinely constitute an OOD distribution at the training semantic level.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS1.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">B.1.3 </span>Population-Level OOD Assessment</h4>

<div id="A2.SS1.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS1.SSS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Settings and Symbols.</span> We selected <math id="A2.SS1.SSS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> auditable open-source MLLMs as test subjects. Our constructed dataset is based on COCO-train and generates OOD data at the semantic level according to OODBench’s division strategy, denoted as ”COCO-train-OOD”.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.SSS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For each model <math id="A2.SS1.SSS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math>, its training overlap rate on ”COCO-train-OOD” is defined as:</p>

Setting the threshold <math id="A2.SS1.SSS3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\varepsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ε</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\varepsilon</annotation></semantics></math> as the maximum acceptable overlap rate, the model’s OOD decision criterion (pre-registered criterion) is defined as:</p>

<div id="A2.SS1.SSS3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">when the 95% upper confidence bound of the training overlap rate for model <math id="A2.SS1.SSS3.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math> does not exceed <math id="A2.SS1.SSS3.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\varepsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ε</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\varepsilon</annotation></semantics></math>, we classify it as ‘treating this data as OOD’ (<math id="A2.SS1.SSS3.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z_{m}=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z_{m}=1</annotation></semantics></math>); if the upper confidence bound exceeds <math id="A2.SS1.SSS3.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\varepsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ε</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\varepsilon</annotation></semantics></math>, it is classified as non-OOD (<math id="A2.SS1.SSS3.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z_{m}=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z_{m}=0</annotation></semantics></math>).</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.SSS3.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS3.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS1.SSS3.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Exact Clopper–Pearson Interval (Frequentist Lower Bound).</span> To estimate, at the population level, the proportion of models that satisfy the preregistered criterion, we treat the set of <math id="A2.SS1.SSS3.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> evaluated open-source models as a finite population. Among them, <math id="A2.SS1.SSS3.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> models satisfy <math id="A2.SS1.SSS3.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z_{m}=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z_{m}=1</annotation></semantics></math>. We therefore compute the lower confidence bound for the binomial proportion based on <math id="A2.SS1.SSS3.p6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> successes out of <math id="A2.SS1.SSS3.p6.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n=N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n=N</annotation></semantics></math> trials. 
<br class="ltx_break">The lower Clopper–Pearson bound is defined as:</p>
</div>

<p id="A2.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">When <math id="A2.I2.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\varepsilon=5\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ε</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\varepsilon=5\%</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A2.I2.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k=49" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>49</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k=49</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A2.I2.i1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n=50" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n=50</annotation></semantics></math>,  <math id="A2.I2.i1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{LCP}=\mathrm{BetaInv}(0.025;49,2)\approx 0.894." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>LCP</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>BetaInv</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0.025</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>49</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≈</mo><mn>0.894</mn></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{LCP}=\mathrm{BetaInv}(0.025;49,2)\approx 0.894.</annotation></semantics></math></p>

</ul>

<div id="A2.SS1.SSS3.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS3.p9.1" class="ltx_p">Therefore, under the criterion of ”<math id="A2.SS1.SSS3.p9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="95\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>95</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">95\%</annotation></semantics></math> upper confidence bound <math id="A2.SS1.SSS3.p9.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\leq 5\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\leq 5\%</annotation></semantics></math> for training overlap rate,” it can be asserted with <math id="A2.SS1.SSS3.p9.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="95\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>95</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">95\%</annotation></semantics></math> confidence that at least approximately <math id="A2.SS1.SSS3.p9.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="89.4\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>89.4</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">89.4\%</annotation></semantics></math> of comparable open-source MLLMs would classify this data as OOD. Even under the stricter criterion of ”<math id="A2.SS1.SSS3.p9.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\leq 2\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\leq 2\%</annotation></semantics></math>,” at least approximately <math id="A2.SS1.SSS3.p9.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="39.3\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>39.3</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">39.3\%</annotation></semantics></math> of models still meet this condition.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.SSS3.p10" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS3.p10.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS1.SSS3.p10.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Bayesian Inference with a Beta(1,1) Prior (Posterior Credible Interval).</span> To validate the above results from a probabilistic reasoning perspective, we employ a uniform prior ”Beta(1,1)” to compute the lower bound of the <math id="A2.SS1.SSS3.p10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="95\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>95</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">95\%</annotation></semantics></math> confidence interval under the posterior distribution:</p>

<div id="A2.SS1.SSS3.p12" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS3.p12.1" class="ltx_p">The result is:</p>
<ul id="A2.I3" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="A2.I3.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span>

<p id="A2.I3.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">When <math id="A2.I3.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\varepsilon=5\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ε</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\varepsilon=5\%</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A2.I3.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k=49" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>49</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k=49</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A2.I3.i1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n=50" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n=50</annotation></semantics></math>,  <math id="A2.I3.i1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L_{\mathrm{Bayes}}=\mathrm{BetaInv}(0.025;50,2)\approx 0.896." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>Bayes</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>BetaInv</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0.025</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>50</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≈</mo><mn>0.896</mn></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_{\mathrm{Bayes}}=\mathrm{BetaInv}(0.025;50,2)\approx 0.896.</annotation></semantics></math></p>

<p id="A2.I3.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">When <math id="A2.I3.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\varepsilon=2\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ε</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\varepsilon=2\%</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A2.I3.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k=27" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>27</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k=27</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A2.I3.i2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n=50" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n=50</annotation></semantics></math>,  <math id="A2.I3.i2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L_{\mathrm{Bayes}}=\mathrm{BetaInv}(0.025;28,24)\approx 0.403." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>Bayes</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>BetaInv</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0.025</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>28</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>24</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≈</mo><mn>0.403</mn></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_{\mathrm{Bayes}}=\mathrm{BetaInv}(0.025;28,24)\approx 0.403.</annotation></semantics></math></p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.SSS3.p13" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS3.p13.1" class="ltx_p">Therefore, from a Bayesian perspective, it can be asserted with <math id="A2.SS1.SSS3.p13.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="95\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>95</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">95\%</annotation></semantics></math> confidence that: when the criterion is ”<math id="A2.SS1.SSS3.p13.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="95\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>95</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">95\%</annotation></semantics></math> upper confidence bound <math id="A2.SS1.SSS3.p13.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\leq 5\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\leq 5\%</annotation></semantics></math>,” at least approximately <math id="A2.SS1.SSS3.p13.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="89.6\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>89.6</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">89.6\%</annotation></semantics></math> of similar models will classify the data as OOD; when the criterion is ”<math id="A2.SS1.SSS3.p13.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\leq 2\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\leq 2\%</annotation></semantics></math>,” at least approximately <math id="A2.SS1.SSS3.p13.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="40.3\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>40.3</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">40.3\%</annotation></semantics></math> of models will classify the data as OOD.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.SSS3.p14" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS3.p14.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS1.SSS3.p14.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Population-Level Conclusion.</span> From two complementary statistical perspectives, the Clopper–Pearson method ensures frequentist coverage, while the Bayesian Beta method provides posterior credibility. Both methods align in direction and magnitude, indicating that, <span id="A2.SS1.SSS3.p14.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">with <math id="A2.SS1.SSS3.p14.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="95\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>95</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">95\%</annotation></semantics></math> confidence, at least approximately <math id="A2.SS1.SSS3.p14.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="89\text{–}90\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>89</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_bold">–</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>90</mn></mrow><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">89\text{–}90\%</annotation></semantics></math> of comparable open-source MLLMs perceive COCO-train-OOD data as semantically OOD during training.</span> These open-source MLLMs encompass diverse families, parameter scales, architectures, and training strategies. Thus, this division can be robustly regarded as an ”out-of-distribution relative to training semantics” sample set at the population level.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS1.SSS4" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">B.1.4 </span>Distributional Equivalence Between COCO-Train-OOD and COCO-Val-OOD</h4>

<div id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Let the random variable be:</p>

</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X</annotation></semantics></math> denotes images and <math id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math> denotes discrete categorical labels. We consider separately:</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="A2.I4" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="A2.I4.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A2.I4.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I4.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="A2.I4.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{\text{train}}(X,C)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mtext>train</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{\text{train}}(X,C)</annotation></semantics></math>: The joint distribution of OOD subsets divided according to OODBench rules on COCO-train.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A2.I4.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A2.I4.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I4.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="A2.I4.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{\text{val}}(X,C)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mtext>val</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{\text{val}}(X,C)</annotation></semantics></math>: The joint distribution of OOD subsets divided according to the same rules on COCO-val.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Section <a href="#A2.SS1.SSS3" title="B.1.3 Population-Level OOD Assessment ‣ B.1 OOD Evidence from Open-Source Models ‣ Appendix B Statistical Evidence for the OOD Nature of OODBench in Modern MLLMs ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.1.3</span></a>, based on the exact Clopper–Pearson interval and the Bayesian Beta(1,1) posterior interval, infers at the <math id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="95\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>95</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">95\%</annotation></semantics></math> confidence level that at least approximately <math id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="89\text{–}90\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>89</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>–</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>90</mn></mrow><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">89\text{–}90\%</annotation></semantics></math> of open-source MLLMs will treat COCO-train-OOD data as OOD for training semantics. To extend this population-level OOD classification to COCO-val-OOD, it is necessary to verify further whether COCO-train-OOD and COCO-val-OOD belong to the same statistical distribution family.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Definition of Distribution Equivalence.</span> We adopt the kernel mean embedding framework and utilize Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) to measure the distance between two joint distributions.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p6.1" class="ltx_p">For any image <math id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>, features are extracted using the self-supervised visual model DINOv2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib72" title="" class="ltx_ref">Oquab et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>

Category labels <math id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c\in C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c\in C</annotation></semantics></math> are represented using one-hot vectors <math id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p8.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e_{c}\in\mathbb{R}^{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>t</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e_{c}\in\mathbb{R}^{t}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A2.E10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\begin{split}k((x,c),(x^{\prime},c^{\prime}))=k_{v}(\phi(x),\phi(x^{\prime}))\cdot\mathds{1}[c=c^{\prime}],\end{split}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mtable displaystyle="true"><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_right" columnalign="right"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><msup><mrow></mrow><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><msup><mrow></mrow><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>v</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><msup><mrow></mrow><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo><mo rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mn>𝟙</mn><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><msup><mrow></mrow><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">]</mo><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\begin{split}k((x,c),(x^{\prime},c^{\prime}))=k_{v}(\phi(x),\phi(x^{\prime}))\cdot\mathds{1}[c=c^{\prime}],\end{split}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(10)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p18" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p18.1" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p18.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math> represents image features extracted via self-supervised visual models <span id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p18.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(e.g.</span>, DINOv2), <math id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p18.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{v}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>v</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{v}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the RBF kernel applied to visual features, and <math id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p18.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathds{1}[\cdot]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>𝟙</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathds{1}[\cdot]</annotation></semantics></math> is the indicator function. This design constructs a block-diagonal joint kernel in the joint space <math id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p18.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(X,C)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(X,C)</annotation></semantics></math>, where kernel values between different categories are zero, making them mutually orthogonal in the RKHS. Meanwhile, similarity within the same category is entirely determined by the RBF kernel of the visual features. In other words, the label variable <math id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p18.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math> participates in joint modeling through the discrete structure of ”intra-class/cross-class,” while the visual subspace provides the intra-class geometric structure.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p19" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p19.1" class="ltx_p">Based on the above joint kernel, the maximum mean displacement (MMD) between the joint distributions <math id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p19.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{\text{train}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>P</mi><mtext>train</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{\text{train}}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p19.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{\text{val}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>P</mi><mtext>val</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{\text{val}}</annotation></semantics></math> can be expressed as:</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p20" class="ltx_para">
<table id="A2.E11" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A2.E11.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\begin{split}\mathrm{MMD}^{2}(P_{\text{train}},P_{\text{val}})=\|\mu_{\text{train}}-\mu_{\text{val}}\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2},\end{split}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mtable displaystyle="true"><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_right" columnalign="right"><mrow><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>MMD</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mtext>train</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mtext>val</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>μ</mi><mtext>train</mtext></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><mtext>val</mtext></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\begin{split}\mathrm{MMD}^{2}(P_{\text{train}},P_{\text{val}})=\|\mu_{\text{train}}-\mu_{\text{val}}\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2},\end{split}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(11)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p21" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p21.1" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p21.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu_{\text{train}},\mu_{\text{val}}\in\mathcal{H}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>μ</mi><mtext>train</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>μ</mi><mtext>val</mtext></msub><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu_{\text{train}},\mu_{\text{val}}\in\mathcal{H}</annotation></semantics></math> represent the kernel mean embeddings of <math id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p21.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{\text{train}}(X,C)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mtext>train</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{\text{train}}(X,C)</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p21.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{\text{val}}(X,C)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mtext>val</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{\text{val}}(X,C)</annotation></semantics></math> in the reproducing kernel Hilbert space <math id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p21.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{H}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{H}</annotation></semantics></math>, respectively. That is, <math id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p21.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu_{P}=\mathbb{E}_{(X,C)\sim P}[\Phi(X,C)]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi>P</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∼</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu_{P}=\mathbb{E}_{(X,C)\sim P}[\Phi(X,C)]</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p21.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Phi</annotation></semantics></math> is the feature map induced by the joint kernel k.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p22" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p22.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p22.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Statistical Test for Distribution Equivalence (Two-Sided Test).</span> We used the equivalence test (TOST) to verify the following hypothesis:</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p23" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="A2.I5" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="A2.I5.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A2.I5.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I5.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="A2.I5.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{H}_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mtext>H</mtext><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{H}_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>: <math id="A2.I5.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{MDD}^{2}(P_{\text{train}},P_{\text{val}})\geq\tau." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>MDD</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mtext>train</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mtext>val</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≥</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{MDD}^{2}(P_{\text{train}},P_{\text{val}})\geq\tau.</annotation></semantics></math> (The difference is at least <math id="A2.I5.i1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> and cannot be considered equivalent)</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A2.I5.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A2.I5.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I5.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="A2.I5.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{H}_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mtext>H</mtext><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{H}_{1}</annotation></semantics></math>: <math id="A2.I5.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{MDD}^{2}(P_{\text{train}},P_{\text{val}})&lt;\tau." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>MDD</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mtext>train</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mtext>val</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{MDD}^{2}(P_{\text{train}},P_{\text{val}})&lt;\tau.</annotation></semantics></math> (The difference is less than <math id="A2.I5.i2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> and can be considered equivalent)</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p24" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p24.1" class="ltx_p">To determine the value of <math id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p24.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math>, we construct a ’homogeneous baseline’ within COCO-train-OOD as follows:</p>
</div>

<div id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p26" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p26.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p26.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the upper bound of the finite-sample fluctuations of <math id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p26.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{MMD}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>MMD</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{MMD}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> observed between two independent samples originating from the same underlying distribution. Consequently, if the <math id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p26.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{MMD}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>MMD</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{MMD}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> between COCO-train-OOD and COCO-val-OOD falls below <math id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p26.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math>, the two partitions can be statistically regarded as independent realizations of a common source distribution, <span id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p26.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">i.e.</span>, as distributionally isomorphic.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p27" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p27.1" class="ltx_p">To further quantify the uncertainty in <math id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p27.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{MMD}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>MMD</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{MMD}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> estimation, we employ a permutation test to construct a reference distribution for its null hypothesis. Specifically, we merge all samples from COCO-train-OOD and COCO-val-OOD into a single dataset, randomly permute their group labels (train/val), and recalculate <math id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p27.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{MMD}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>MMD</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{MMD}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> based on the permuted grouping structure. Repeating this process B times (B=500 in this experiment) yields the empirical permutation distribution of <math id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p27.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{MMD}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>MMD</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{MMD}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> under the null hypothesis <math id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p27.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{H}_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mtext>H</mtext><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{H}_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> (equivalence of the two distributions):</p>
</div>

<p id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p42.1" class="ltx_p">At the significance level <math id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p42.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=0.05" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.05</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=0.05</annotation></semantics></math>, we reject the null hypothesis <math id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p42.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{H}_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mtext>H</mtext><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{H}_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> —that the difference is at least <math id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p42.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> —and accept the equivalence hypothesis <math id="A2.SS1.SSS4.p42.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{H}_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mtext>H</mtext><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{H}_{1}</annotation></semantics></math>. This confirms that COCO-train-OOD and COCO-val-OOD are statistically distributionally equivalent within the prescribed tolerance. Since a model’s OOD response is fundamentally determined by the degree to which the test data deviates from its training semantic distribution, and train-OOD has already been shown in the previous section to constitute semantic OOD for open-source MLLMs, the statistical indistinguishability between val-OOD and train-OOD indicates that both deviate from the training distribution to the same order of magnitude. Consequently, COCO-val-OOD should exhibit the same OOD behavior for open-source MLLMs and can thus be regarded as semantic OOD data equivalent to train-OOD.</p>

</section>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.2 </span>OOD Evidence from Closed-Source Models</h3>

<div id="A2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Problem Setup and Assumptions.</span> Let</p>
<ul id="A2.I7" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="A2.I7.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A2.I7.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I7.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="A2.I7.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D_{\text{ID}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mtext>ID</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{\text{ID}}</annotation></semantics></math>: Conventional ID test set.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A2.I7.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A2.I7.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I7.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="A2.I7.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D_{\text{OOD}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mtext>OOD</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{\text{OOD}}</annotation></semantics></math>: A semantic OOD test set constructed according to OODBench semantic rules (non-main semantic objects, semantic variants, and anomalous image–category pairings), with its image subset sourced from COCO-val.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In the open-source model section, we have established the following two key premises:</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="A2.I8" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="A2.I8.ix1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="A2.I8.ix1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I8.ix1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.I8.ix1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Training Out-of-Distribution Properties.
<br class="ltx_break"></span>By calculating the semantic overlap rate between the training corpora of open-source MLLMs and COCO-train-OOD, and combining precise binomial intervals with Bayesian credible intervals using uniform priors, we obtain the following: At the <math id="A2.I8.ix1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="95\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>95</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">95\%</annotation></semantics></math> confidence level, at least <math id="A2.I8.ix1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="90\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>90</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">90\%</annotation></semantics></math> of open-source models exhibit an overlap rate with COCO-train-OOD not exceeding <math id="A2.I8.ix1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5\%</annotation></semantics></math>. This result indicates that, <span id="A2.I8.ix1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">from the perspective of training distribution, COCO-train-OOD can be robustly regarded as OOD data for the collection of open-source models.</span></p>
</div></li>
<li id="A2.I8.ix2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="A2.I8.ix2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I8.ix2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.I8.ix2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Distributional Equivalence Between COCO-train-OOD and COCO-val-OOD.
<br class="ltx_break"></span>Under the same semantic division rules, we construct COCO-train-OOD and COCO-val-OOD and perform an equivalence test in the joint space of image features and category labels using kernel MMD combined with the TOST procedure. The results indicate that <span id="A2.I8.ix2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">the two subsets are statistically indistinguishable and can be regarded as two independent samples drawn from the same underlying distribution, <span id="A2.I8.ix2.p1.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">i.e.</span>, they exhibit distributional equivalence.</span></p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Therefore, in subsequent reasoning, it can be directly treated as a known premise:</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="A2.I9" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="A2.I9.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A2.I9.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I9.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.I9.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">For the open-source model collection <math id="A2.I9.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}_{\text{open}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_bold">open</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}_{\text{open}}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A2.I9.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D_{\text{OOD}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_bold">OOD</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{\text{OOD}}</annotation></semantics></math> is OOD in terms of the training distribution.</span></p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.p6.1" class="ltx_p">For closed-source models (such as GPT-4o, Gemini, <span id="A2.SS2.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">etc.</span>), since their training data is inaccessible, we cannot directly determine whether <math id="A2.SS2.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D_{\text{OOD}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mtext>OOD</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{\text{OOD}}</annotation></semantics></math> falls outside their training distribution. To address this, we employ behavioral consistency inference:</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.p7" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="A2.I10" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="A2.I10.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A2.I10.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I10.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">First, inductively derive observable ”open-source model OOD behavioral patterns”— <span id="A2.I10.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">i.e.</span>, OOD behavioral signatures—from the inference results of open-source models on <math id="A2.I10.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D_{\text{OOD}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mtext>OOD</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{\text{OOD}}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A2.I10.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A2.I10.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I10.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Subsequently, verify whether the behavior of closed-source models on the same data <math id="A2.I10.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D_{\text{OOD}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mtext>OOD</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{\text{OOD}}</annotation></semantics></math> aligns with these known ”open-source OOD behavioral patterns”.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.p8.1" class="ltx_p">Suppose its behavior aligns with the OOD behavioral signature of the open-source model. In that case, it can be inferred that the closed-source model’s response pattern on <math id="A2.SS2.p8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D_{\text{OOD}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mtext>OOD</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{\text{OOD}}</annotation></semantics></math> corresponds to its performance on typical OOD data. This indicates that it exhibits behavioral characteristics consistent with OOD scenarios on that dataset.</p>
</div>
<section id="A2.SS2.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">B.2.1 </span>Behavioral Statistics and Performance Degradation</h4>

<div id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For any model <math id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math> (either open-source or closed-source) and for any data split <math id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S\in\{ID,OOD\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>O</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S\in\{ID,OOD\}</annotation></semantics></math>, we define the basic classification metrics as follows:</p>

<p id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p8.1" class="ltx_p">As demonstrated by the aforementioned distribution homogeneity analysis, for the open-source model ensemble, <math id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D_{\text{OOD}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mtext>OOD</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{\text{OOD}}</annotation></semantics></math> is indeed OOD on the training distribution. We can further abstract a set of observable OOD behavioral patterns from its performance on <math id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p8.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D_{\text{OOD}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mtext>OOD</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{\text{OOD}}</annotation></semantics></math>, namely the OOD behavioral signatures of open-source models.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p9.1" class="ltx_p">Let the open-source model collection be denoted as <math id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}_{\text{open}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mtext>open</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}_{\text{open}}</annotation></semantics></math>. <p id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p11.1" class="ltx_p">This interval <math id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p11.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I_{(k)}^{\text{gap}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>I</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mtext>gap</mtext></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I_{(k)}^{\text{gap}}</annotation></semantics></math> represents the typical performance degradation range exhibited by the open-source model on the <math id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p11.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>th performance metric dimension for <math id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p11.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D_{\text{OOD}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mtext>OOD</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{\text{OOD}}</annotation></semantics></math> instances that have been confirmed as OOD.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p12" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p12.1" class="ltx_p">Let the set of degeneracy bands for all metric dimensions be denoted as:</p>
</div>

<div id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p14" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p14.1" class="ltx_p">We refer to <math id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p14.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math> as the behavioral signature of the open-source model when processing semantic OOD inputs. It reflects the systematic decline pattern in the model’s performance from ID to OOD when confronted with semantic OOD. It is crucial to emphasize that Signature <math id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p14.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math> is not the definition of OOD itself; rather, the definition of OOD stems from data construction and training distribution analysis. Signature <math id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p14.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math> is merely an observable ”behavioral fingerprint” of OOD’s effect on model behavior.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS2.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">B.2.2 </span>Behavioral Verification of Closed-Source Models</h4>

<div id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For closed-source model <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math>, we cannot observe its training data. Therefore, we employ behavioral-side statistical tests to address two questions:</p>
<ul id="A2.I11" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="A2.I11.ix1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="A2.I11.ix1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I11.ix1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Does the closed-source model exhibit significant ID <math id="A2.I11.ix1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math> OOD degradation on <math id="A2.I11.ix1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D_{\text{OOD}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mtext>OOD</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{\text{OOD}}</annotation></semantics></math>?</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A2.I11.ix2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="A2.I11.ix2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I11.ix2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Does the degradation magnitude of the closed-source model align with the OOD behavioral signature <math id="A2.I11.ix2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math> of the open-source model?</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(1) Significance Test of Performance Differences Between Closed-Source Models in ID vs OOD.</span> For each metric dimension <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>, we define the same degeneracy measure for closed-source models:</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<table id="A2.E21" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

</table>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta_{c,obs}^{(k)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta_{c,obs}^{(k)}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the observed degradation amount calculated based on the valid ID/OOD classification.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">To verify whether this represents OOD behavior rather than random fluctuations, we construct the following hypothesis test for each <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="A2.I12" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="A2.I12.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A2.I12.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I12.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Null hypothesis <math id="A2.I12.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>: The closed-source model exhibits no performance difference between ID and OOD:</p>
<table id="A2.Ex7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">

</table>
</div></li>
<li id="A2.I12.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A2.I12.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I12.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Alternative hypothesis <math id="A2.I12.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_{1}</annotation></semantics></math>: The closed-source model performs worse on OOD (degradation exists):</p>

</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p7.1" class="ltx_p">We achieve this through a permutation test of ID and OOD sample labels. Under the null hypothesis <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>, ID/OOD labels should be interchangeable, yielding the null distribution of the degradation amount <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta_{c}^{(k)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>c</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta_{c}^{(k)}</annotation></semantics></math>. If the observed <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta_{c}^{(k)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>c</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta_{c}^{(k)}</annotation></semantics></math> falls in the extreme tail of this distribution (<span id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">e.g.</span>, beyond the top <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p7.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5\%</annotation></semantics></math>), reject <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p7.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> and conclude that degradation is significant. Therefore, we randomly permute the ID/OOD labels of the original data and recalculate the degradation amount for each permutation:</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p8" class="ltx_para">

</div>

</div>

</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p13" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p13.1" class="ltx_p">when <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p13.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{c}^{(k)}&lt;0.05" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>p</mi><mi>c</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0.05</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{c}^{(k)}&lt;0.05</annotation></semantics></math>, we reject <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p13.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> as statistically significant. That is, the closed-source model exhibits significant ID <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p13.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math> OOD performance degradation on <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p13.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D_{\text{OOD}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mtext>OOD</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{\text{OOD}}</annotation></semantics></math>, which is a typical behavioral signal when semantic OOD is applied to the model.</p>
</div>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A2.F8.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 8</span>: </span><span id="A2.F8.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">This figure illustrates the distribution of degradation amounts under the null hypothesis <math id="A2.F8.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> (no performance difference between ID and OOD) and the positions of the observed values. As illustrated, for both closed-source models and across all metrics, the observed degradation falls in the extreme tail of the permutation distribution. The permutation p-values are all below <math id="A2.F8.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10^{-3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10^{-3}</annotation></semantics></math>, and out of 2000 permutations, none produced a degradation larger than the observed value.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p14" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p14.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p14.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Observation Conclusions:</span> For closed-source models (GPT-4o and Gemini), we calculated the observed measure of ID <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p14.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math> OOD performance degradation <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p14.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta_{c,obs}^{(k)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta_{c,obs}^{(k)}</annotation></semantics></math> across five performance dimensions (Accuracy, F1, Precision, Recall, MCC). We constructed the corresponding null hypothesis distribution based on <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p14.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B=2000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2000</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B=2000</annotation></semantics></math> label permutations. Figure <a href="#A2.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ B.2.2 Behavioral Verification of Closed-Source Models ‣ B.2 OOD Evidence from Closed-Source Models ‣ Appendix B Statistical Evidence for the OOD Nature of OODBench in Modern MLLMs ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> presents violin plots illustrating the distribution of degradation amounts and the positions of observed values for each metric under the null hypothesis <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p14.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> (no performance difference between ID and OOD). It is evident that for all metrics and both closed-source models, the observed degradation consistently resides in the extreme tail of the permutation distribution: their permutation p-values are all below <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p14.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10^{-3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10^{-3}</annotation></semantics></math>, and across all 2000 permutations, not a single permutation resulted in degradation exceeding the actual observed values. From a statistical inference perspective, this implies: at the commonly used significance level <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p14.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=0.05" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.05</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=0.05</annotation></semantics></math>, the stricter <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p14.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=0.01" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.01</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=0.01</annotation></semantics></math>, and even <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p14.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=0.001" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.001</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=0.001</annotation></semantics></math>, we have sufficient evidence to reject the null hypothesis <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p14.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H_{0}:T_{c,ID}^{(k)}=T_{c,OOD}^{(k)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>T</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi>T</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>O</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_{0}:T_{c,ID}^{(k)}=T_{c,OOD}^{(k)}</annotation></semantics></math> and accept the one-tailed alternative hypothesis <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p14.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H_{0}:T_{c,ID}^{(k)}&gt;T_{c,OOD}^{(k)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>T</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>&gt;</mo><msubsup><mi>T</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>O</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_{0}:T_{c,ID}^{(k)}&gt;T_{c,OOD}^{(k)}</annotation></semantics></math>. In other words, under the current data and testing framework, <span id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p14.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">the closed-source model exhibits statistically significant performance differences between the ID subset and the OOD-labeled subset, and this difference is highly unlikely to be caused by random label perturbations.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p15" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p15.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p15.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(2) Consistency of OOD Behavioral Signatures Between Closed-Source and Open-Source Models.</span> We aggregate the bootstrapped degradation values of the open-source models to obtain population-level statistics:</p>
<ul id="A2.I13" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="A2.I13.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A2.I13.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I13.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Open-source mean degradation: <math id="A2.I13.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu_{\text{open}^{(k)}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>μ</mi><msup><mtext>open</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu_{\text{open}^{(k)}}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A2.I13.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A2.I13.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I13.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Open-source variability (natural fluctuation scale): <math id="A2.I13.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{\text{open}}^{(k)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>σ</mi><mtext>open</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{\text{open}}^{(k)}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p16" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p16.1" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p16.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu_{\text{open}^{(k)}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>μ</mi><msup><mtext>open</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu_{\text{open}^{(k)}}</annotation></semantics></math> expresses the typical degradation magnitude of open-source models on semantic OOD; <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p16.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{\text{open}}^{(k)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>σ</mi><mtext>open</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{\text{open}}^{(k)}</annotation></semantics></math> represents the natural fluctuation scale of degradation within the open-source community (model variance + sample noise). Furthermore, we define this natural fluctuation scale as the tolerance threshold:</p>
</div>

<div id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p21" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="A2.I14" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="A2.I14.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A2.I14.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I14.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">If <math id="A2.I14.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta^{(k)}=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>δ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\delta^{(k)}=0</annotation></semantics></math>: closed-source degradation = open-source average degradation;</p>
