<div id="A2.I14.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I14.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">If <math id="A2.I14.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\delta^{(k)}|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msup><mi>δ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\delta^{(k)}|</annotation></semantics></math> is small (<span id="A2.I14.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">e.g.</span>, within <math id="A2.I14.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm\eta_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>±</mo><msub><mi>η</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm\eta_{k}</annotation></semantics></math>): closed-source degradation and open-source degradation are ”of the same order of magnitude”;</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A2.I14.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A2.I14.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I14.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">If <math id="A2.I14.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\delta^{(k)}|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msup><mi>δ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\delta^{(k)}|</annotation></semantics></math> is much larger than <math id="A2.I14.i3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\eta_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>η</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\eta_{k}</annotation></semantics></math>, closed-source behavior and open-source OOD behavior are significantly inconsistent.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p22" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p22.1" class="ltx_p">To obtain the distribution of <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p22.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta^{(k)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>δ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\delta^{(k)}</annotation></semantics></math> and its <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p22.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="90\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>90</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">90\%</annotation></semantics></math> confidence interval, we perform <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p22.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math> bootstrap resamples on both ID and OOD samples. In each resample, we simultaneously estimate the following quantities:</p>
<ul id="A2.I15" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="A2.I15.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A2.I15.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I15.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.I15.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Degradation of the closed-source model:
<br class="ltx_break"><math id="A2.I15.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta_{c,b}^{(k)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta_{c,b}^{(k)}</annotation></semantics></math>, denoting the performance degradation from ID to OOD for the closed-source model in the <math id="A2.I15.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>b</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math>th resample;</span></p>
</div></li>
<li id="A2.I15.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A2.I15.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I15.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.I15.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">The average degradation of the open-source model population:
<br class="ltx_break"><math id="A2.I15.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu_{open,b}^{(k)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>μ</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu_{open,b}^{(k)}</annotation></semantics></math></span>, representing the average degradation of the open-source model population during the <math id="A2.I15.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>b</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math>th resampling (averaged across the two open-source models).</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>

<div id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p26" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p26.1" class="ltx_p">Equivalence test hypotheses:</p>
<ul id="A2.I16" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="A2.I16.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A2.I16.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I16.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Null hypothesis <math id="A2.I16.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> (non-equivalence):</p>
<table id="A2.Ex12" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">

<p id="A2.I16.i1.p1.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.I16.i1.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">i.e.</span>, the difference between closed-source degradation and open-source degradation on metric <math id="A2.I16.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> is at least <math id="A2.I16.i1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\eta_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>η</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\eta_{k}</annotation></semantics></math>, indicating behavioral non-equivalence.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A2.I16.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A2.I16.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I16.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Alternative hypothesis <math id="A2.I16.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> (equivalence):</p>

<div id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p27" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p27.1" class="ltx_p">In practice, we construct a confidence interval using <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p27.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{\delta^{(k)}_{b}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msubsup><mi>δ</mi><mi>b</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{\delta^{(k)}_{b}\}</annotation></semantics></math> and employ CI to implement the TOST decision. We adopt the standard equivalent test framework, using a <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p27.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="90\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>90</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">90\%</annotation></semantics></math> confidence interval at a significance level of <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p27.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=0.05" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.05</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=0.05</annotation></semantics></math>. Specifically, we extract the 5th and 95th percentiles from <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p27.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{\delta^{(k)}_{b}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msubsup><mi>δ</mi><mi>b</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{\delta^{(k)}_{b}\}</annotation></semantics></math> to obtain the <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p27.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="90\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>90</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">90\%</annotation></semantics></math> CI:</p>

<div id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p31" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p31.1" class="ltx_p">At the <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p31.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=0.05" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.05</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=0.05</annotation></semantics></math> significance level, we reject the null hypothesis <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p31.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H_{0}:|\delta^{(k)}|\geq\eta_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msup><mi>δ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>≥</mo><msub><mi>η</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_{0}:|\delta^{(k)}|\geq\eta_{k}</annotation></semantics></math> and accept <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p31.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H_{1}:|\delta^{(k)}|&lt;\eta_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msup><mi>δ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>&lt;</mo><msub><mi>η</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_{1}:|\delta^{(k)}|&lt;\eta_{k}</annotation></semantics></math>. This indicates that: 
<br class="ltx_break">The difference between closed-source degradation and open-source average degradation is constrained within the ”open-source natural fluctuation scale <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p31.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{\text{open}}^{(k)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>σ</mi><mtext>open</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{\text{open}}^{(k)}</annotation></semantics></math>” in dimension <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p31.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>, rendering it equivalent to open-source OOD behavior.</p>

<p id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p32.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p32.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Observational Conclusion:</span> In this study, we selected InternVL2-8B and InternVL2.5-8B as open-source reference models. We then employed the TOST equivalence testing framework to evaluate the behavioral consistency of closed-source models (GPT-4o and Gemini) on semantic OOD data. <div id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p34" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p34.1" class="ltx_p">As shown, the <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p34.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="90\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>90</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">90\%</annotation></semantics></math> confidence intervals for all five metrics fall within the corresponding tolerance ranges <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p34.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(-\eta_{k},\eta_{k})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>η</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>η</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(-\eta_{k},\eta_{k})</annotation></semantics></math>, <span id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p34.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">i.e.</span>, Equ. <a href="#A2.E26" title="Equation 26 ‣ B.2.2 Behavioral Verification of Closed-Source Models ‣ B.2 OOD Evidence from Closed-Source Models ‣ Appendix B Statistical Evidence for the OOD Nature of OODBench in Modern MLLMs ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">26</span></a>, satisfying the equivalence criterion. In other words, across all performance dimensions, the ID <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p34.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math> OOD degradation of GPT-4o fluctuates at the same order of magnitude as the average degradation of the open-source model population, without exceeding the natural variability exhibited by the open-source models.</p>

<p id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p35.2" class="ltx_p">Similarly, all metrics satisfy Equ. <a href="#A2.E26" title="Equation 26 ‣ B.2.2 Behavioral Verification of Closed-Source Models ‣ B.2 OOD Evidence from Closed-Source Models ‣ Appendix B Statistical Evidence for the OOD Nature of OODBench in Modern MLLMs ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">26</span></a>, indicating that Gemini’s degradation also falls stably within the natural fluctuation range of degradation observed in open-source communities.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p36" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p36.1" class="ltx_p">In summary, GPT-4o and Gemini are statistically equivalent to the open-source OOD behavioral signature across all five performance dimensions—Accuracy, F1, Precision, Recall, and MCC. Their ID <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p36.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math> OOD degradation magnitudes remain within the same order of magnitude as those of the open-source models, exhibiting no deviations beyond the natural variability scale <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p36.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\sigma_{\text{open}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>σ</mi><mtext>open</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\sigma_{\text{open}})</annotation></semantics></math>. These findings indicate that the closed-source models display OOD response patterns on our semantic OOD data that are consistent with those observed in the open-source models.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p37" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p37.1" class="ltx_p">From the two types of analyses above, we obtain the following conclusions.
Combining (1) the significance tests on ID vs. OOD performance differences for closed-source models and (2) the consistency between closed-source behavior and the open-source OOD behavioral signature, we observe that:</p>
<ul id="A2.I17" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="A2.I17.ix1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(1).</span> 
<div id="A2.I17.ix1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I17.ix1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Closed-source models exhibit statistically significant ID <math id="A2.I17.ix1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math> OOD performance degradation on <math id="A2.I17.ix1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D_{\text{OOD}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mtext>OOD</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{\text{OOD}}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A2.I17.ix2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(2).</span> 
<div id="A2.I17.ix2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I17.ix2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The magnitude of this degradation across all key metrics falls within the natural OOD variability range of the open-source models, consistent with the open-source OOD behavioral signature.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p38" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p38.1" class="ltx_p">Thus, on the same semantic OOD dataset, the ID <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p38.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math> OOD degradation patterns of closed-source models—both in direction and magnitude—align with those of open-source models on known OOD tests. This supports the view that <span id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p38.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">closed-source models treat <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p38.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D_{\text{OOD}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_bold">OOD</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{\text{OOD}}</annotation></semantics></math> as OOD data in a manner equivalent to open-source models.</span></p>
</div>

<section id="A3" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix C </span>Differences between OODBench and Hard Sample</h2>

<div id="A3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Hard samples refer to data instances that exhibit high uncertainty, low confidence, or are prone to misclassification during model training or inference. Although they originate from the training distribution (in-distribution, ID), they typically reside in the tail or low-density regions — the marginal distribution portion. Typical hard samples include: blurred, occluded, or low-resolution images; instances with ambiguous semantic boundaries or highly similar categories (<span id="A3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">e.g.</span>, dogs and wolves); and minority class samples under long-tail distributions. They essentially represent “challenging points” within the distribution, often amenable to fitting through enhanced generalization capabilities, sample reweighting, or increased sample size. In contrast, this paper refines the definition of out-of-distribution (OOD) samples from a human perception perspective, categorizing them into two types: (1) objects in an image that are non-main objects and semantically unrelated to the main object; and (2) variants or abnormal forms of the target object. These samples fundamentally represent “semantic OOD” data that multimodal large models struggle to cover during semantic learning.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To investigate the distinction between OODBench and hard samples, we drew inspiration from the OHEM method <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shrivastava et al., 2016</a>)</cite> to construct a set of hard samples on the COCO dataset and evaluated them using nine state-of-the-art models. By comparing the performance (<span id="A3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">i.e.</span>, behavioral patterns) of different models on hard samples versus OODBench, we aim to reveal the differences between the two. In the data partitioning process, we adopted an offline hard sample mining approach, with the specific algorithm detailed in Algorithm <a href="#alg1" title="Algorithm 1 ‣ Appendix C Differences between OODBench and Hard Sample ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. First, a sufficiently converged detector is selected to define sample difficulty (YOLOv8-xlarge <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ultralytics, 2023</a>)</cite> was used as the detector in this study). Perform inference on the input image to generate a set of candidate boxes (proposals). For each candidate box, compute the prediction distribution <math id="A3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(c\mid x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(c\mid x)</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="A3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c\in\{1,\dots,C\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c\in\{1,\dots,C\}</annotation></semantics></math>, and determine the predicted class <math id="A3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{c}=\argmax p(c\mid x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>c</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>arg</mi><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>max</mi></mrow><mo>⁡</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{c}=\argmax p(c\mid x)</annotation></semantics></math>. Subsequently, we computed a hardness score for each sample, using the commonly employed Focal Loss <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al., 2017</a>)</cite> value as the metric:</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<table id="A3.E27" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A3.E27.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\begin{split}h(x)=(1-p(\hat{c}\mid x))^{\gamma}\cdot(-\log p(\hat{c}\mid x)),\quad\gamma=2\end{split}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mtable displaystyle="true"><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_right" columnalign="right"><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>c</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>γ</mi></msup><mo rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">−</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>c</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><mrow><mi>γ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\begin{split}h(x)=(1-p(\hat{c}\mid x))^{\gamma}\cdot(-\log p(\hat{c}\mid x)),\quad\gamma=2\end{split}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(27)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="A3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">among these, scores for easily classifiable samples are significantly suppressed, retaining only hard samples. Next, for all proposals within each image, we group them by predicted category and select the top-k samples with the highest hardness within each category to add to the candidate hard sample list. After traversing the entire dataset, the top-k hard samples from each category within every image are aggregated. Finally, the hard sample list is globally sorted by hardness score, and the top-q% samples from each category are selected to form the final hard sample set.</p>
</div>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_float"><span id="alg1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Algorithm 1</span> </span> Hard Sample Mining via Focal Loss Scoring</figcaption>

<div id="A3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#A3.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ Appendix C Differences between OODBench and Hard Sample ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> demonstrates the performance of ID data, OODBench data, and hard samples across nine state-of-the-art multimodal large language models (MLLMs). As shown in Figure <a href="#A3.F10" title="Figure 10 ‣ Appendix C Differences between OODBench and Hard Sample ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>, we plotted the performance differences of each model on hard samples and OOD-H compared to in-distribution data, then sorted the results in ascending order based on the magnitude of performance decline on hard samples. Analysis reveals significant variations in the challenge posed by hard samples across models: for instance, Gemini’s performance declined by only 5.96%, while Qwen2.5-VL-Instruct experienced a substantial 33.62% drop. This indicates that hard samples remain in-distribution data, with performance degradation primarily dependent on a model’s robustness and generalization capabilities. Specifically, certain models exhibited pronounced performance degradation on specific hard samples (<span id="A3.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">e.g.</span>, DeepSeek-VL-7B-Chat, Llama-3.2-11B-Vision-Instruct, and Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct, all of which exceeded a 30% decline), while others remained largely unaffected (<span id="A3.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">e.g.</span>, Gemini and InternVL2-8B). In contrast, OODBench-defined OOD samples reveal a consistent performance decline across all nine models, with even robust models failing to significantly mitigate this effect. For example, GPT-4o experienced a 27.65% performance drop on OOD samples. This result indicates that OOD samples exhibit a distribution shift property consistent across models, rather than relying solely on individual model robustness.</p>
</div>
<section id="A3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.1 </span>Statistical distinction between Hard and OOD</h3>

<div id="A3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Setup.</span> For each model <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m=1,\dots,M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m=1,\dots,M</annotation></semantics></math> (here <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M=9" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>9</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M=9</annotation></semantics></math>), we compute the performance degradation on hard samples <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta_{\text{Hard}}(m)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mtext>Hard</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta_{\text{Hard}}(m)</annotation></semantics></math> and the performance degradation on our dataset <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta_{\text{OOD}}(m)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mtext>OOD</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta_{\text{OOD}}(m)</annotation></semantics></math>. We analyze the following aspects: (i) variability across models, (ii) alignment of performance degradation patterns, and (iii) overlap rate between data partitioned by OODBench and OHEM.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Evidence 1 — Variance Test on Full Sets (Hard vs OOD)</span> 
<br class="ltx_break">We compare the variance across models using an F-test:</p>
<table id="A3.E28" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A3.E28.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\begin{split}F=\frac{\text{Var}(\Delta_{\text{Hard}})}{\text{Var}(\Delta_{\text{OOD}})}\sim F(\nu_{1},\nu_{2}),\nu_{1}=\nu_{2}=M-1\end{split}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mtable displaystyle="true"><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_right" columnalign="right"><mrow><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mtext>Var</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mtext>Hard</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mtext>Var</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mtext>OOD</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>ν</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>ν</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>ν</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>ν</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\begin{split}F=\frac{\text{Var}(\Delta_{\text{Hard}})}{\text{Var}(\Delta_{\text{OOD}})}\sim F(\nu_{1},\nu_{2}),\nu_{1}=\nu_{2}=M-1\end{split}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(28)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A3.SS1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">In our experiments, <math id="A3.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F(8,8)=4.59" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>4.59</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F(8,8)=4.59</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A3.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=0.0227" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.0227</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=0.0227</annotation></semantics></math>, indicating that the variance in performance degradation caused by Hard samples is significantly greater than that caused by OOD samples.
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A3.SS1.p2.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Explanation:</span> Hard samples exhibit greater model dependency, while OOD samples induce a more consistent (model-independent) performance degradation.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Evidence 2 — Correlation on full sets (Hard vs OOD)
<br class="ltx_break"></span>We measure the alignment of performance degradation patterns through correlation analysis:</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<table id="A3.E29" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A3.E29.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\begin{split}r=\text{corr}(\Delta_{\text{Hard}},\Delta_{\text{OOD}})\end{split}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mtable displaystyle="true"><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_right" columnalign="right"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mtext>corr</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mtext>Hard</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mtext>OOD</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\begin{split}r=\text{corr}(\Delta_{\text{Hard}},\Delta_{\text{OOD}})\end{split}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(29)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">We observe negative correlations (Pearson r = -0.65, p = 0.059; Spearman <math id="A3.SS1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> = -0.58, p = 0.099). These results indicate inconsistencies in the failure patterns of models on Hard and OOD samples: models exhibiting significant performance degradation on Hard samples do not necessarily show similar degradation on OOD samples, and vice versa. Furthermore, from the performance trend lines shown in Figure <a href="#A3.F10" title="Figure 10 ‣ Appendix C Differences between OODBench and Hard Sample ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>, we observe an X-shaped decline pattern, where models exhibit significant fluctuations or reversals at certain points. This phenomenon aligns with the correlation test results, further validating the misaligned patterns of performance shifts across Hard and OOD samples. The X-shaped trend lines reflect the models’ markedly divergent responses to different sample types (Hard vs. OOD).</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.SS1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Hypotheses</span></p>
<ul id="A3.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="A3.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A3.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="A3.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{H_{0}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐇</mi><mn>𝟎</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{H_{0}}</annotation></semantics></math> (Hard Hypothesis): The OODBench dataset shares the same distribution as the in-distribution Hard subset. In other words, the statistical characteristics of its cross-model performance degradation vector <math id="A3.I1.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta V" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>V</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta V</annotation></semantics></math> (including variance and correlation/alignment with the baseline Hard) should fall within the “empirical distribution of the Hard subset.”</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A3.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A3.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="A3.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{H_{1}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐇</mi><mn>𝟏</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{H_{1}}</annotation></semantics></math> (OOD Hypothesis): OODBench does not belong to the Hard subset, and the same-distribution assumption does not hold; its statistical characteristics will significantly deviate from the “Hard baseline.”</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS1.p7.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.SS1.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Test statistics. </span> Record the cross-model performance decline vector (ID performance - Hard sample performance) for the baseline Hard model as <math id="A3.SS1.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta_{\text{Hard}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mtext>Hard</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta_{\text{Hard}}</annotation></semantics></math> (length equal to the number of models <math id="A3.SS1.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M=9" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>9</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M=9</annotation></semantics></math>).</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS1.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS1.p8.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.SS1.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Resample details.</span> We performed resampling based on Algorithm <a href="#alg1" title="Algorithm 1 ‣ Appendix C Differences between OODBench and Hard Sample ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> to construct the empirical baseline for the Hard subset. Specifically, B=1000 independent samples were conducted, each randomly selecting 500 Hard samples from the COCO validation pool. All samples were selected according to a unified criterion: scoring using focal loss and choosing the top-k samples within each category. Each sampling process was independent, yielding distinct sets of 1000 Hard samples, thereby ensuring the randomness and diversity of the baseline distribution.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS1.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS1.p9.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.SS1.p9.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Evidence 3 — Empirical variance test</span></p>
<ul id="A3.I2" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="A3.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A3.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.I2.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Statistical Measure</span>: <math id="A3.I2.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s^{2}_{\text{OOD}}=\text{Var}(\Delta_{\text{OOD}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mtext>OOD</mtext><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mtext>Var</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mtext>OOD</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s^{2}_{\text{OOD}}=\text{Var}(\Delta_{\text{OOD}})</annotation></semantics></math></p>
</div></li>
<li id="A3.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A3.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.I2.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Test Direction (one side)</span>: left tail. Hard samples are typically more model-dependent, exhibiting greater cross-model variance; if <math id="A3.I2.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s^{2}_{\text{OOD}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mtext>OOD</mtext><mn>2</mn></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s^{2}_{\text{OOD}}</annotation></semantics></math> is significantly smaller, reject <math id="A3.I2.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{H_{0}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐇</mi><mn>𝟎</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{H_{0}}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A3.I2.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A3.I2.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.I2.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.I2.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Baseline Construction</span>: Resample <math id="A3.I2.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H^{(b)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H^{(b)}</annotation></semantics></math> from the COCO validation set using the same mechanism as Algorithm <a href="#alg1" title="Algorithm 1 ‣ Appendix C Differences between OODBench and Hard Sample ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>’s rule.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A3.I2.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A3.I2.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.I2.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.I2.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Baseline Distribution</span>: <math id="A3.I2.i4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{b}=\text{Var}(\Delta_{H^{(b)}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mtext>Var</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{b}=\text{Var}(\Delta_{H^{(b)}})</annotation></semantics></math></p>
</div></li>
<li id="A3.I2.i5" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A3.I2.i5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.I2.i5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.I2.i5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Decision</span>: If the empirical p-value <math id="A3.I2.i5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{p}_{\text{emp}}&lt;0.05" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mtext>emp</mtext></msub><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0.05</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{p}_{\text{emp}}&lt;0.05</annotation></semantics></math> (<span id="A3.I2.i5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">i.e.</span>, OOD falls below the 5th percentile of the Hard baseline distribution), reject <math id="A3.I2.i5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{H_{0}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐇</mi><mn>𝟎</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{H_{0}}</annotation></semantics></math>, concluding that the candidate set exhibits greater model-agnostic consistency in cross-model score drops, consistent with OOD characteristics. Results are shown in Figure <a href="#A3.F11" title="Figure 11 ‣ C.1 Statistical distinction between Hard and OOD ‣ Appendix C Differences between OODBench and Hard Sample ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a> (left). The empirical p-value is less than 1/(B+1) (<span id="A3.I2.i5.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">i.e.</span>, <math id="A3.I2.i5.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{p}_{\text{emp}}&lt;0.001" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mtext>emp</mtext></msub><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0.001</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{p}_{\text{emp}}&lt;0.001</annotation></semantics></math>), strongly rejecting <math id="A3.I2.i5.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{H_{0}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐇</mi><mn>𝟎</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{H_{0}}</annotation></semantics></math>. This indicates that the statistical characteristics of the candidate set significantly deviate from the Hard baseline.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS1.p10" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS1.p10.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.SS1.p10.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Evidence 4 — Empirical correlation test</span></p>
<ul id="A3.I3" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="A3.I3.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A3.I3.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.I3.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.I3.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Statistical Measure</span>: <math id="A3.I3.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{\text{OOD}}=\text{corr}(\Delta_{\text{Hard}},\Delta_{\text{OOD}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mtext>OOD</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mtext>corr</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mtext>Hard</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mtext>OOD</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{\text{OOD}}=\text{corr}(\Delta_{\text{Hard}},\Delta_{\text{OOD}})</annotation></semantics></math></p>
</div></li>
<li id="A3.I3.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A3.I3.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.I3.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.I3.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Test Direction (one side)</span>: left tail. Hard vs Hard drop-off modes are typically non-negative or positively aligned; if <math id="A3.I3.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{\text{OOD}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>r</mi><mtext>OOD</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{\text{OOD}}</annotation></semantics></math> is significantly low, reject <math id="A3.I3.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{H_{0}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐇</mi><mn>𝟎</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{H_{0}}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A3.I3.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A3.I3.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.I3.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.I3.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Baseline Construction</span>: Resample <math id="A3.I3.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math> hard subsets <math id="A3.I3.i3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H^{(b)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H^{(b)}</annotation></semantics></math> from the COCO validation set and compute their correlation with the baseline hard set.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A3.I3.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A3.I3.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.I3.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.I3.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Baseline Distribution</span>: <math id="A3.I3.i4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{b}=\text{corr}(\Delta_{\text{Hard}},\Delta_{\text{OOD}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mtext>corr</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mtext>Hard</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mtext>OOD</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{b}=\text{corr}(\Delta_{\text{Hard}},\Delta_{\text{OOD}})</annotation></semantics></math></p>
</div></li>
<li id="A3.I3.i5" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A3.I3.i5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.I3.i5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.I3.i5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Decision</span>: If the empirical p-value <math id="A3.I3.i5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{p}_{\text{emp}}&lt;0.05" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mtext>emp</mtext></msub><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0.05</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{p}_{\text{emp}}&lt;0.05</annotation></semantics></math> (<span id="A3.I3.i5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">i.e.</span>, <math id="A3.I3.i5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{\text{OOD}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>r</mi><mtext>OOD</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{\text{OOD}}</annotation></semantics></math> falls below the 5th percentile of the Hard baseline distribution), reject <math id="A3.I3.i5.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{H_{0}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐇</mi><mn>𝟎</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{H_{0}}</annotation></semantics></math>, indicating that the candidate set does not align with Hard’s failure pattern, consistent with OOD’s ”different failure mode.” Results are shown in Figure <a href="#A3.F11" title="Figure 11 ‣ C.1 Statistical distinction between Hard and OOD ‣ Appendix C Differences between OODBench and Hard Sample ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a>: The middle subfigure displays the distribution of Pearson correlation coefficients from 1000 resamples, all exceeding 0.9; The right subfigure shows the distribution of Spearman correlation coefficients, all exceeding 0.8. In contrast, the OOD correlations with Hard are -0.65 (Pearson) and -0.58 (Spearman), significantly below the Hard baseline distribution. The empirical p-value is less than 0.001, strongly rejecting <math id="A3.I3.i5.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{H_{0}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐇</mi><mn>𝟎</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{H_{0}}</annotation></semantics></math> and further demonstrating that the statistical characteristics of the candidate set significantly deviate from the Hard baseline.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<figure id="A3.F11" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18094v1/std_correlation_score_distribution.png" id="A3.F11.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/95;" width="476" height="95" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A3.F11.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 11</span>: </span><span id="A3.F11.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">The figure displays the empirical distribution results for variance (left), Pearson correlation coefficient (center), and Spearman correlation coefficient (right). The x-axis of the variance subplot represents variance values, while the x-axes of the Pearson and Spearman subplots respectively denote the corresponding correlation coefficients. The y-axes of all three subplots indicate sample sizes. The red dashed lines in each subplot mark the statistical values of the out-of-distribution (OOD) data.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A3.SS1.p11" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS1.p11.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.SS1.p11.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Evidence 5 — Overlap Rate Between Hard Sample and OODBench</span></p>
<ul id="A3.I4" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="A3.I4.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A3.I4.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.I4.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.I4.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Statistical Measure</span>: We calculated the overlap rate between the full COCO-H dataset (5,079 samples) in OODBench and the Hard sample collection (2,641 samples) obtained by sampling according to Algorithm 1. This metric evaluates the consistency between our classified OOD data and the hard samples generated by conventional hard sample mining methods.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A3.I4.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A3.I4.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.I4.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.I4.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Results</span>: Statistical analysis revealed only 206 overlapping samples, accounting for 0.0406% of the total COCO-H dataset and 0.0780% of the total hard samples.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A3.I4.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A3.I4.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.I4.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.I4.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Conclusion</span>: Such a low overlap rate indicates that the OOD data categorized by OODBench fundamentally differs from the hard samples obtained through traditional hard sample mining methods. In other words, OODBench captures more universally applicable out-of-distribution patterns rather than conventional in-distribution hard samples.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS1.p12" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS1.p12.1" class="ltx_p">Taken together, the five lines of evidence consistently demonstrate that the OODBench data cannot be regarded as conventional hard samples. Evidence 1 (variance test on full sets) shows that performance degradation on Hard samples exhibits significantly larger variance across models than on OOD, indicating stronger model dependency for Hard. Evidence 2 (correlation analysis) reveals negative associations between Hard and OOD drop patterns, further corroborated by the X-shaped trend lines, highlighting misaligned failure modes. Evidence 3 (empirical variance test) confirms that the variance of OOD drops is significantly smaller than the empirical Hard baseline, rejecting <math id="A3.SS1.p12.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{H_{0}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐇</mi><mn>𝟎</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{H_{0}}</annotation></semantics></math>. Evidence 4 (empirical correlation test) further establishes that OOD correlations with Hard (-0.65, -0.58) fall far below the Hard-vs-Hard baseline (all <math id="A3.SS1.p12.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&gt;0.9" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0.9</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&gt;0.9</annotation></semantics></math> Pearson, <math id="A3.SS1.p12.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&gt;0.8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0.8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&gt;0.8</annotation></semantics></math> Spearman), again strongly rejecting <math id="A3.SS1.p12.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{H_{0}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐇</mi><mn>𝟎</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{H_{0}}</annotation></semantics></math>. Finally, Evidence 5 (overlap rate) shows that the intersection between OODBench samples and mined hard samples is minimal (206 out of 5,079), underscoring their fundamental distinction.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS1.p13" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS1.p13.1" class="ltx_p">Across all five evidences, the results are significant and directionally consistent: OODBench captures distributional shifts and model-agnostic failure modes, whereas Hard samples remain in-distribution and model-dependent. Therefore, our OOD data are not merely hard samples but instead represent a fundamentally different category aligned with out-of-distribution characteristics.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A4" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix D </span>Differences between OODBench and Hallucination</h2>

<div id="A4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Out-of-Distribution (OOD) may cause hallucinations, but hallucinations are not necessarily caused by OOD.</span> We analyse in depth the differences between OOD and hallucinations in terms of concepts, interrelationships and experimental results to demonstrate the distinctiveness of the both.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Hallucination definitions in the Large Vision- Language Model (LVLM)</span>: Hallucination in LVLM denotes a disagreement between factual content of images and corresponding generated textual content, akin to the solely textual hallucination encountered in large language models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2024a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bai et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. 
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A4.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Definition of OOD</span>: Traditionally, OOD is defined as a test example originating from a distribution different from the training data <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hendrycks and Gimpel, 2017</a>)</cite>. In recent studies <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Averly and Chao, 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>, the OOD detector identifies misclassified examples labelled as OOD Data to improve the safety and reliability of deep learning models in practical applications.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In LVLMs, hallucination refers to the inconsistency between the generated text description and the visual content. Our experiment shows that OOD data does not necessarily lead to hallucinations and that it is not fully equivalent to hallucinations. As shown in Tab. <a href="#S5.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 5.2 Evaluation Setup ‣ 5 Experiment ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, OOD data does not necessarily trigger hallucinations. For example, on the OOD-H data, the accuracy of GPT-4o was 65.13%, implying that 100% - 65.13% = 34.87% of the OOD data led to hallucinations, while the remaining 65.13% of the OOD data did not trigger hallucinations. This indicates that there is not a one-to-one correspondence between OOD and hallucinations. Second, the causes of hallucinations are multiple, and not all hallucinations are caused by OOD data. For example, the ID data in Tab. <a href="#S5.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 5.2 Evaluation Setup ‣ 5 Experiment ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> also triggered hallucinations. This phenomenon was also verified in the BAP experiments in Tab. <a href="#S5.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 5.3 Main Results Analysis ‣ 5 Experiment ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. Taking GPT-4o as an example, we asked questions on ID data according to Basic-to-Advanced Progress, including existential description, counting description, and logical reasoning, and the performance was 94.84%, 48.26%, and 30.83% in decreasing order. This indicates that as the complexity of the inference task increases, the model becomes more hallucinatory and the match between the generated text and the visual content decreases. The results of the above experiments demonstrate that there is some intersection between OOD and hallucinations, but they are not equivalent.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Prior research <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2023</a>)</cite> has shown that CoT (Chain of Thought) is an effective way to alleviate hallucinations. In our experiments, CoT did not perform as well on OOD data. For example, in Tab. <a href="#S5.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 5.2 Evaluation Setup ‣ 5 Experiment ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, we observed that several models such as DeepSeek-VL-7B-Chat, DeepSeek-VL2-Small, Llama3.2-11B-Vision, Qwen2-7B-Instruct, and GPT-4o failed to improve their performance, but instead, their performance decreased to different degrees after using CoT. This phenomenon may stem from the fact that the distribution of the OOD data deviates from the training distribution, which makes CoT reason with out-of-distribution data as the starting point, thus reinforcing false assumptions, amplifying the inference bias, and ultimately reducing the model performance. We begin by hypothesising that there is a high degree of overlap between the data in OODBench and the hallucinations. Further, CoT, as a typical method to mitigate the hallucination problem, should improve the model performance on this benchmark. However, the experimental results were contrary to expectations: the model performance decreased rather than increased after the introduction of CoT. This phenomenon directly refutes our initial hypothesis that the OODBench data highly overlaps with hallucinations. Instead, it experimentally validates that there is an essential difference between our divided OOD dataset and hallucinations. Together, these experimental results demonstrate that the OOD dataset we constructed is significantly different from the hallucination.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
<section id="A5" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix E </span>Ablation Study of the Generalized OOD Detector and Hyperparameter T</h2>

<section id="A5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">E.1 </span>Ablation study of different types of generalized OOD Detector</h3>

<div id="A5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In order to explore the impact of different types of OOD detectors on the performance of downstream tasks when dividing OOD data under the generalized OOD detection framework, we designed and conducted a series of systematic ablation experiments. In the specific setup, we selected GroupViT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al., 2022</a>)</cite> and LiT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhai et al., 2022</a>)</cite> to gradually replace the original CLIP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Radford et al., 2021</a>)</cite> with BLIP2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhai et al., 2022</a>)</cite> to re-divide the samples in the COCO dataset into OOD, and we constructed two new sets of division data. Subsequently, we input the three sets of delineation results (<span id="A5.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">i.e.</span>, original division + division of the two alternative detectors) into two open-source multimodal models (InternVL2, Qwen2-VL) and two closed-source models (Gemini, GPT-4o), respectively, for consistency testing to assess the impact of different generalised OOD detectors on the downstream performance performance.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">It should be noted that in order to control the testing overhead, the original OODBench benchmark introduces a random downsampling strategy when the number of samples exceeds 6,000. In order to avoid the possible data distribution bias introduced by downsampling, we retain all the samples judged as OOD, <span id="A5.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">i.e.</span>, we do not perform the downsampling operation again when we use GroupViT with LiT for reclassification. At the same time, in order to ensure the fairness of the experiment, we continue to use the sample sets corresponding to the CLIP and BLIP2 classification results in the initial benchmark to ensure the consistency of the processing flow among the three groups.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">For ease of presentation, we define the three datasets as follows: 
<br class="ltx_break">   The data divided by CLIP and BLIP2 are recorded as Group <span id="A5.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">I</span>. 
<br class="ltx_break">   The data divided by BLIP2 and GroupViT are recorded as Group <span id="A5.SS1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">II</span>. 
<br class="ltx_break">   The data divided by GroupViT and LiT are recorded as Group <span id="A5.SS1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">III</span>.</p>
</div>
