<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="A5.T8.10" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 8</span>: </span><span id="A5.T8.11" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Impact of replacing generalized OOD detectors on the downstream performance of different multimodal models. We compare the accuracy differences (<math id="A5.T8.m30" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta</annotation></semantics></math>) of data divided by different combinations of detectors—Group <span id="A5.T8.11.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">I</span> (CLIP + BLIP2), Group <span id="A5.T8.11.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">II</span> (BLIP2 + GroupViT), and Group <span id="A5.T8.11.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">III</span> (GroupViT + LiT)—across four representative VLMs (Qwen2-VL-7B-Instruct, InternVL2-8B, Gemini, and GPT-4o). Group <span id="A5.T8.11.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">I</span> is used as the baseline, and the performance drop or gain of Group <span id="A5.T8.11.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">II</span> and Group <span id="A5.T8.11.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">III</span> is reported accordingly. The results show that although different detectors induce slight variance in OOD data division, their impact on downstream model performance is minimal, supporting the replaceability of generalized OOD detectors in the OODBench framework.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A5.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We first evaluated Qwen2-VL by taking the performance of group <span id="A5.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">I</span> data as the baseline and calculating the accuracy difference (<math id="A5.SS1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>δ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\delta</annotation></semantics></math>) between group <span id="A5.SS1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">II</span> and group <span id="A5.SS1.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">III</span> data under the model relative to the baseline. The experimental results show that on Qwen2-VL, the accuracy of group II and group <span id="A5.SS1.p4.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">III</span> data decreases by 1.11% and 1.43%, respectively, compared with that of group <span id="A5.SS1.p4.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">I</span>. On Gemini, it improves by 0.86% and 0.06%, respectively, and the performance difference between the three groups of data on InternVL and GPT-4o is also minimal, and the details of the values are shown in Tab. <a href="#A5.T8" title="Table 8 ‣ E.1 Ablation study of different types of generalized OOD Detector ‣ Appendix E Ablation Study of the Generalized OOD Detector and Hyperparameter T ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>. In the Time column, the time superscript indicates the number of graphics cards used in the test, and we used NVIDIA L40s graphics cards in the testing phase.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">These results show that although there is some discriminative difference between the different OOD detectors when dividing the samples, this difference does not trigger a significant performance bias in the evaluation of the downstream multimodal model. <span id="A5.SS1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">It is experimentally verified that the generalized OOD detectors in the OODBench division process are replaceable.</span> In other words, as long as the detector itself has good class discrimination ability, it can effectively classify OOD data for large visual language models.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">In addition, we note that Tong <span id="A5.SS1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">et al.</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tong et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tong et al., 2023</a>)</cite>. raised the issue of CLIP failure transfer, suggesting that current large VLMs may inherit transfer flaws from adopting CLIP as a visual or text encoder. The results are in the Tab. <a href="#A5.T8" title="Table 8 ‣ E.1 Ablation study of different types of generalized OOD Detector ‣ Appendix E Ablation Study of the Generalized OOD Detector and Hyperparameter T ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> shows that the model’s performance in the OOD detection task remains stable even when the CLIP is replaced with other classifiers, ruling out the possibility of further failure transfer of the CLIP into the VLM in OOD detection. It is thus concluded that the performance bottleneck of VLM in such tasks does not originate from CLIP itself. This finding helps to rule out the hypothesis of further spreading of ‘CLIP failure transfer‘ in VLMs, suggesting that a combination of more factors influences the performance of VLMs in this kind of task.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A5.F12" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18094v1/ood_detector_num_ablation.svg" id="A5.F12.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:333/333;" width="333" height="333"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A5.F12.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 12</span>: </span><span id="A5.F12.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Impact of the number of generalized OOD detectors on the quality of OOD data division under the cross-validation mechanism. The horizontal axis indicates the number of detectors involved in the division process (ranging from 1 to 4), while the vertical axis shows the corresponding Accuracy and F1 score (%) obtained by evaluating the divided OOD data on multiple mainstream VLMs. The results demonstrate that using a single detector yields the highest performance but suffers from potential bias. Incorporating two detectors significantly reduces this bias, producing OOD data more aligned with the VLMs’ potential OOD distribution. However, increasing the number of detectors beyond two offers limited benefits and may introduce instability, as evidenced by performance rebound and eventual convergence.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">E.2 </span>Ablation studies with different numbers of generalized OOD Detectors</h3>

<div id="A5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To further investigate the effect of different numbers of generalized OOD detectors on the division of OOD data under the cross-validation mechanism, we conducted ablation experiments on the number of detectors. We selected four models, CLIP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Radford et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, BLIP2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2023b</a>)</cite>, GroupViT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, and LiT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhai et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, as generalized OOD detectors, and sequentially increased the number of detectors involved in the division in a fixed order. Consistent with the OOD detector type ablation experiment <a href="#A5.SS1" title="E.1 Ablation study of different types of generalized OOD Detector ‣ Appendix E Ablation Study of the Generalized OOD Detector and Hyperparameter T ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.1</span></a>, to avoid introducing additional bias, we did not perform downsampling operations on the OOD data divided by the above models to maintain the consistency of the division process. To assess the impact of the number of detectors on the OOD data division results, we tested the OOD data divided by different numbers of detectors on several mainstream VLMs. We visualised the results in the form of a line graph (shown in Figure <a href="#A5.F12" title="Figure 12 ‣ E.1 Ablation study of different types of generalized OOD Detector ‣ Appendix E Ablation Study of the Generalized OOD Detector and Hyperparameter T ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a>). The horizontal axis of the graph represents the number of detectors involved in the division, and the vertical axis represents the accuracy and F1 score obtained from testing on each VLM.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The experimental results show that when only a single OOD detector (number 1) is used, each VLM reaches the highest value in both Accuracy and F1, which indicates that a single detector may bring about model bias, which in turn leads to a mismatch between the divided OOD data and the potential OOD distribution of the large VLMs. When the number of detectors is increased to 2, the performance of each large VLM decreases significantly, indicating that the cross-validation mechanism can mitigate the error brought about by single-detector bias to some extent, thus obtaining data that more closely fits the OOD distribution of the large VLM. However, when the number of detectors is further increased to 3, the performance of all six VLMs except InternVL2.5-8B shows a performance rebound, <span id="A5.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">i.e.</span>, the data divided by three detectors generally performs higher than that of 2 detectors in terms of Accuracy and F1. Nonetheless, this performance rebound is still significantly lower than that seen with the single detector division. When the number of detectors reaches 4, we observe that the test performance is almost the same as with three detectors, suggesting that further increases in the number of detectors do not lead to substantial improvement in division, and that the division effect tends to stabilise.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Combining the results of the experiments with two to four detectors, <span id="A5.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">we found that a higher number of OOD detectors is not better. With two detectors, the division results are closest to the potential OOD distribution of the major VLMs.</span> Continuing to increase the number of detectors may instead introduce additional uncertainty, which leads to the division of data deviating from the potential OOD distribution of the major large VLMs and gradually converging. Based on performance and division stability considerations, we ultimately chose to use <span id="A5.SS2.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">2</span> OOD detectors to construct the default configuration of the OOD data division scheme in OODBench.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A5.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">E.3 </span>The selection of the threshold T</h3>

<div id="A5.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In the process of collecting OOD data, we define that when the probability of an instance category is lower than the threshold <math id="A5.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math>, it is considered a detection failure, and thus, the instance category is considered OOD data. In order to investigate the effect of different thresholds <math id="A5.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> on the division of OOD data, we conducted <math id="A5.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> ablation experiments. Considering that Llama <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Touvron et al., 2023</a>)</cite> is currently the most popular Large Language Model, we chose Llama-3.2-Vision <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dubey et al., 2024</a>)</cite> as the test model. When <math id="A5.SS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> is larger than <math id="A5.SS3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.05" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.05</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.05</annotation></semantics></math>, there is too much OOD data division, so we set <math id="A5.SS3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="A5.SS3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.05" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.05</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.05</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A5.SS3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.01" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.01</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.01</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="A5.SS3.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.005" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.005</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.005</annotation></semantics></math> to control the amount of OOD data. The experimental results are shown in Tab. <a href="#A5.T9" title="Table 9 ‣ E.3 The selection of the threshold T ‣ Appendix E Ablation Study of the Generalized OOD Detector and Hyperparameter T ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>: when <math id="A5.SS3.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T=0.05" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.05</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T=0.05</annotation></semantics></math>, the accuracy difference between OOD-S and OOD-H is <math id="A5.SS3.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="7.44" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>7.44</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">7.44</annotation></semantics></math>; when <math id="A5.SS3.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T=0.01" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.01</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T=0.01</annotation></semantics></math>, the difference decreases to <math id="A5.SS3.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.86" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1.86</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.86</annotation></semantics></math>; and when <math id="A5.SS3.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T=0.005" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.005</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T=0.005</annotation></semantics></math>, the difference further decreases to <math id="A5.SS3.p1.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.73" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1.73</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.73</annotation></semantics></math>. As the value of <math id="A5.SS3.p1.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> decreases, the boundary of the distributions between OOD-S and OOD-H becomes more blurred. In terms of the number of OOD data, the decrease in the value of <math id="A5.SS3.p1.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> leads to a decrease in the number of OOD-S from 25,798 to about 23,500 and a significant decrease in the number of OOD-H from 9,882 to 4,274. To ensure that the model divides the OOD data with a high degree of differentiation, we finally set <math id="A5.SS3.p1.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="A5.SS3.p1.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.05" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.05</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.05</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>

<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix F </span>OODBench Sub-Dataset Performance</h2>

<div id="A6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Subdataset classification performance.</span> Tab. <a href="#A6.T10" title="Table 10 ‣ Appendix F OODBench Sub-Dataset Performance ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>, Tab. <a href="#A6.T11" title="Table 11 ‣ Appendix F OODBench Sub-Dataset Performance ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a>, Tab. <a href="#A6.T12" title="Table 12 ‣ Appendix F OODBench Sub-Dataset Performance ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a> and Tab. <a href="#A6.T13" title="Table 13 ‣ Appendix F OODBench Sub-Dataset Performance ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a> show the performance of the different models on publicly available datasets collected in natural and autonomous driving scenarios, respectively. Where, OOD-S‘ and OOD-H‘ denote the initial benchmark datasets. In the Time column, the time superscript indicates the number of graphics cards used in the test, and we used NVIDIA L40s graphics cards in the testing phase.</p>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="A6.T13.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 13</span>: </span><span id="A6.T13.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Performance on Cityscapes-ID-OOD.<span id="A6.T13.7.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> We report the performance of the </span>10<span id="A6.T13.7.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> leading VLMs on OODBench. All models perform significantly lower on OOD-H than on ID.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
<div id="A6.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A6.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Subdataset BAP performance.</span> Tab. <a href="#A6.T14" title="Table 14 ‣ Appendix F OODBench Sub-Dataset Performance ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">14</span></a>,  <a href="#A6.T15" title="Table 15 ‣ Appendix F OODBench Sub-Dataset Performance ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">15</span></a>,  <a href="#A6.T16" title="Table 16 ‣ Appendix F OODBench Sub-Dataset Performance ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">16</span></a>, and  <a href="#A6.T17" title="Table 17 ‣ Appendix F OODBench Sub-Dataset Performance ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">17</span></a> show the evaluation results of the BAP metrics on four datasets, namely COCO, LVIS, nuScenes, and Cityscapes, respectively. The BAP metrics progressively increase the complexity of the questions from the perspective of task construction, and consist of Existence, Counting, and Logic Reasoning, with the corresponding performance evaluation metrics of E-Acc, C-Acc, and L-Acc, respectively.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The results of the four datasets show a consistent trend. Under the same question type, as the data distribution migrates from ID to OOD-S to OOD-H, the model performance generally decreases. This phenomenon indicates that the performance of the multimodal large language model degrades significantly when the data distribution deviates from the training distribution, reflecting that its generalization ability in dealing with complex environments is still limited.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.p4.1" class="ltx_p">On the other hand, while keeping the test data unchanged, when the complexity of questioning is gradually increased from Existence to Counting to Logic Reasoning, the accuracy of the model on the three corresponding metrics (E-Acc, C-Acc, and L-Acc) also shows a decreasing trend, which indicates that the higher the requirement of reasoning ability is, the more difficult it is for the model to answer correctly.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Specifically, Tab. <a href="#A6.T14" title="Table 14 ‣ Appendix F OODBench Sub-Dataset Performance ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">14</span></a> to <a href="#A6.T17" title="Table 17 ‣ Appendix F OODBench Sub-Dataset Performance ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">17</span></a> systematically show the performance of major mainstream VLMs on the four datasets of COCO, LVIS, nuScenes, and Cityscapes. The results are generally consistent, further validating the generality of the two trends mentioned above. This indicates that current VLMs still have significant performance bottlenecks when facing more challenging inference tasks and more complex data distributions.</p>
</div>

<section id="A7" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix G </span>Effect of Model Scale on OODBench Performance</h2>

<div id="A7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To further analyze the performance of models of different scales on OODBench under the same architecture, we conducted a systematic comparison of different parameter scales within the same model family. Specifically, we selected the representative Qwen2-VL series. We performed experiments on the complete sets and subsets of the four domains covered by OODBench (COCO, LVIS, nuScenes, Cityscapes) for its 2B and 7B versions. The results are shown in Table <a href="#A7.T18" title="Table 18 ‣ Appendix G Effect of Model Scale on OODBench Performance ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">18</span></a>: The 2B model achieved accuracy scores of 80.6, 64.0, and 81.2 on the OOD-H metrics for COCO, nuScenes, and Cityscapes, respectively, all surpassing the 7B model’s scores of 77.7, 57.6, and 75.4. However, on the LVIS dataset, the 7B model slightly outperformed the 2B model. These results reveal a distinct mixed trend, <span id="A7.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">indicating that model size does not maintain a monotonically increasing relationship with OOD robustness. Increasing parameter size does not consistently enhance model performance under semantic OOD conditions.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="A7.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.p2.1" class="ltx_p">This phenomenon is further validated in larger-scale models. For instance, as shown in Tables <a href="#S5.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 5.2 Evaluation Setup ‣ 5 Experiment ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>,  <a href="#A6.T10" title="Table 10 ‣ Appendix F OODBench Sub-Dataset Performance ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>,  <a href="#A6.T11" title="Table 11 ‣ Appendix F OODBench Sub-Dataset Performance ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a>,  <a href="#A6.T12" title="Table 12 ‣ Appendix F OODBench Sub-Dataset Performance ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a>, and  <a href="#A6.T13" title="Table 13 ‣ Appendix F OODBench Sub-Dataset Performance ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a>, models like GPT-4o and Gemini, which have significantly more parameters than 7B, do not systematically outperform smaller-scale models on OODBench. Overall, expanding model scale cannot fundamentally resolve semantic OOD issues. The root cause lies in the fact that when test samples deviate from the support domain of training data in the joint image-text distribution, their OOD characteristics remain independent of model scale and thus do not naturally disappear with increased capacity.</p>
</div>

<section id="A8" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix H </span>CLIP and BLIP2 visualization distribution logits on coco val</h2>

<div id="A8.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A8.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Why is OODBench Challenging?</span> The appearance of OOD data is usually caused by semantic shift or covariate shift, which means that the generation mechanism of the test data has changed from the training data. Although a model performs well on the training set, it may show degraded or unstable performance when faced with a change in the data distribution. Models usually lack sufficient robustness to such changes, especially when dealing with changes that are not supported by explicit labels or historical data. We divide the OODBench data containing covariate shift through the OOD detector, which has shifted its data distribution despite sharing the same label space as the training data. Deep learning models often give high-confidence predictions or even make very confident false predictions when dealing with these data. The fundamental reason why OODBench poses a challenge to models is that it does not follow the distributional assumptions of the training data.
In contrast, OOD data from the real world is highly uncertain and diverse. When confronted with these data, models typically lack the necessary knowledge and ability to make accurate predictions, which can lead to misclassification or high-confidence false predictions. We shows a visualization of the distribution of logits predicted by VLMs when confronted with real-world data.</p>
</div>
<div id="A8.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Figures <a href="#A8.F14" title="Figure 14 ‣ Appendix H CLIP and BLIP2 visualization distribution logits on coco val ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">14</span></a> and <a href="#A8.F15" title="Figure 15 ‣ Appendix H CLIP and BLIP2 visualization distribution logits on coco val ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">15</span></a> show the results of CLIP and BLIP2 for computing logits on the COCO validation set for 80 labeled categories. Figure <a href="#A8.F13" title="Figure 13 ‣ Appendix H CLIP and BLIP2 visualization distribution logits on coco val ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a>, on the other hand, summarises the logit results of CLIP and BLIP2 on the COCO validation set for 80 categories. As shown in Figure <a href="#A8.F13" title="Figure 13 ‣ Appendix H CLIP and BLIP2 visualization distribution logits on coco val ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a>, the logits distribution shows a double peak, appearing on both sides of the distribution, which indicates that the CLIP and BLIP2 models have high confidence in the instance category. However, the single peak on the far left side of Figure <a href="#A8.F13" title="Figure 13 ‣ Appendix H CLIP and BLIP2 visualization distribution logits on coco val ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a> indicates that both models also have high confidence in determining instance-category mismatches, resulting in high-confidence false predictions.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A8.F13" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2"><img src="2602.18094v1/coco_val_total_logits_CLIP.png" id="A8.F13.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:238/128;" width="238" height="128" alt="Refer to caption"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2"><img src="2602.18094v1/coco_val_total_logits_BLIP2.png" id="A8.F13.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:238/127;" width="238" height="127" alt="Refer to caption"></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A8.F13.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 13</span>: </span><span id="A8.F13.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Logistically visualized distributions of CLIP (top image) and BLIP2 (bottom image) on coco val.</span></figcaption>
</figure>

<section id="A9" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix I </span>OODBench Data and Case Demonstration</h2>

<div id="A9.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A9.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we show some of the data examples constructed by OODBench, covering OOD scenarios divided from datasets such as COCO, LVIS, nuScenes, and Cityscapes. Figures <a href="#A9.F16" title="Figure 16 ‣ Appendix I OODBench Data and Case Demonstration ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">16</span></a> and <a href="#A9.F17" title="Figure 17 ‣ Appendix I OODBench Data and Case Demonstration ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">17</span></a> show the associated visualisations. Through these examples, we aim to help readers visualise the characteristics of different types of out-of-distribution data and the challenges they pose under different tasks and perceptual conditions faced by large multimodal models.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A9.F16" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18094v1/coco_nuscenes_example.png" id="A9.F16.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_portrait" style="aspect-ratio:310/460;" width="310" height="460" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A9.F16.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 16</span>: </span><span id="A9.F16.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Sample OOD instances from the COCO and nuScenes datasets are divided by OODBench. These examples illustrate diverse out-of-distribution categories across different scenarios and environments.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="A9.F17" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18094v1/lvis_cityscapes_example.png" id="A9.F17.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_portrait" style="aspect-ratio:310/446;" width="310" height="446" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A9.F17.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 17</span>: </span><span id="A9.F17.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Sample OOD instances divided from the LVIS and Cityscapes datasets by OODBench. The samples highlight distributional shifts in object-centric.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
<div id="A9.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A9.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To further demonstrate the applicability and challenge of OODBench, we constructed typical examples on four datasets, COCO, LVIS, nuScenes, and Cityscapes, which are shown in Figs. <a href="#A9.F18" title="Figure 18 ‣ Appendix I OODBench Data and Case Demonstration ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">18</span></a>, <a href="#A9.F19" title="Figure 19 ‣ Appendix I OODBench Data and Case Demonstration ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">19</span></a>, <a href="#A9.F20" title="Figure 20 ‣ Appendix I OODBench Data and Case Demonstration ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">20</span></a>, <a href="#A9.F21" title="Figure 21 ‣ Appendix I OODBench Data and Case Demonstration ‣ OODBench: Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Large Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">21</span></a>, respectively. Each set of examples covers a variety of question types, including standard question answering, Chain-of-Thought prompting, and tasks such as existential, counting, and logical reasoning under BAP metrics. These cases visualise the challenges of perception and reasoning in large multimodal models in different out-of-distribution scenarios.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A9.F18" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18094v1/Case_Demonstration_COCO.png" id="A9.F18.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_portrait" style="aspect-ratio:381/525;" width="381" height="525" alt="Refer to caption">

<section id="A10" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix J </span>Limitations</h2>

<div id="A10.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A10.p1.1" class="ltx_p">While OODBench offers a fully automated covariate‐shift benchmark for VLMs, it remains limited in scope. First, it is confined to general natural and autonomous driving domains and does not cover other real‐world domains (<span id="A10.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">e.g.</span>, medical imaging, satellite imagery). In these domains, researchers must redefine appropriate OOD types based on their specific semantic structures, task requirements, and distribution characteristics. Simultaneously, the performance of specialized detectors directly impacts the quality of initial screening, while subsequent expert evaluations (<span id="A10.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">e.g.</span>, in medical settings) may incur additional labor costs. Therefore, the OOD definition within this framework should not be directly applied to the aforementioned domains. Second, it focuses solely on static vision data and omits temporal or multimodal variations. Third, it lacks extreme environmental conditions (<span id="A10.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">e.g.</span>, severe weather, low light). Extending OODBench to additional domains, dynamic data, and challenging environmental factors will be an important direction for future work.</p>
</div>
</section>
